body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the aorta and common carotid, the course and relations of the external carotid, its eight branches one by one, the venous drainage and the lymphatics. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Right common carotid from the brachiocephalic trunk; left directly from the aortic arch.
Carotid bifurcation: carotid triangle, upper border of the thyroid cartilage, C3 to C4 disc.
External carotid begins anteromedial to the internal carotid and ends lateral to it.
It terminates in the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.
Eight branches: superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal, maxillary.
Superior thyroid: infrahyoid, superior laryngeal, cricothyroid, glandular.
Lingual artery is divided into three parts by the hyoglossus; four branches: suprahyoid, dorsal lingual, sublingual, deep lingual.
Facial artery crosses the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter and ends as the angular artery.
Ascending pharyngeal is the smallest branch of the external carotid.
Stylomastoid branch of the posterior auricular artery enters the stylomastoid foramen.
Maxillary artery: three parts (mandibular, pterygoid, pterygopalatine), five branches each; the middle meningeal enters the foramen spinosum.
Angular vein = supratrochlear + supraorbital. It becomes the facial vein.
Retromandibular vein = superficial temporal + maxillary. Anterior division to the facial vein, posterior division to the external jugular.
External jugular drains into the subclavian vein; internal jugular continues from the sigmoid sinus and joins the subclavian to form the brachiocephalic.
Facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins and the pterygoid plexus: a route for infection to reach the brain.
Lymph: upper face to preauricular, mid face to submandibular, lower lip and chin to submental; then cervical nodes and the jugular trunks.

high_yield.html: Carotid bifurcation: upper border of the thyroid cartilage, C3-C4, in the carotid triangle. The ECA starts anteromedial to the ICA and ends lateral to it. The ICA has no branches in the neck; the ECA has eight.
ECA branches: 'Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students': Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal.
The ECA ends in the parotid gland, behind the neck of the mandible, as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. Smallest branch = ascending pharyngeal.
Facial artery crosses the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter (pulse point), runs tortuously to the angle of the mouth and ends as the angular artery.
Maxillary artery: 3 parts by the lateral pterygoid; key branch = middle meningeal through the foramen spinosum.

Retromandibular vein = superficial temporal + maxillary veins; anterior division → facial vein (→ common facial → IJV); posterior division + posterior auricular → external jugular. In the parotid, from superficial to deep: facial nerve → retromandibular vein → ECA.

Danger triangle of the face: the facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins and the pterygoid plexus (deep facial vein) → squeezing a spot near the nose can seed cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Lymph: upper face and lateral lids → preauricular/parotid; cheeks, upper lip, lateral nose → submandibular; lower lip centre, chin, tongue tip → submental; all then to the deep cervical chain.
Superficial temporal artery in front of the tragus is a pulse point and the biopsy site for giant cell (temporal) arteritis.

deeper.title: The danger area of the face
deeper.html:
The lecture's warning about infection spreading to the cavernous sinus has a name: the danger triangle, running from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose. Infection of the upper lip, the vestibule of the nose or the eyelids can travel along the angular, supraorbital and supratrochlear veins to the ophthalmic veins, which drain straight into the cavernous sinus. The second route is the deep facial vein into the pterygoid plexus, which receives an emissary vein from the cavernous sinus through the foramen ovale. That is why squeezing a spot in this area is not as harmless as it looks.

Sources: Radiopaedia, Facial-cavernous anastomoses; Radiopaedia, Pterygoid venous plexus.

deeper.title: Why the internal carotid has no branches in the neck
deeper.html:
A quick way to tell the two carotids apart in a dissection or an image: the external carotid gives off branches almost immediately, while the internal carotid gives none in the neck at all and heads straight for the carotid canal to supply the brain. If a vessel in the neck is branching, it is the external carotid.

Source: AnatomyZone, External carotid artery.

deeper.title: The pterygoid plexus as a pump
deeper.html:
The veins of the pterygoid plexus have valves, and the plexus works as a small pump: contractions of the lateral pterygoid squeeze it and help push venous blood back toward the heart. It also explains why a badly placed dental injection into the plexus can leak blood into the orbit and give the patient a black eye.

Sources: Radiopaedia, Pterygoid venous plexus; Brainscape, Veins of head and neck.

deeper.title: Why the facial artery is so tortuous
deeper.html:
The facial artery takes a winding path across the face rather than a straight one. The slack lets the vessel stretch as the mandible moves and the face changes expression, without the artery being put under tension. Its pulse can be felt where it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter, a standard clinical pulse point.

Sources: Kenhub, The external carotid artery and its branches; lecture slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Fliyou's lecture: the situation and embryology of the brainstem, its connections, the external configuration of the midbrain, pons and medulla, the emergence of the cranial nerves, the internal configuration with the reticular formation, tracts and fourth ventricle, the blood supply, functions and clinical aspects. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Brainstem: midbrain, pons, medulla, in the posterior cranial fossa on the clivus.
Ten of twelve cranial nerves arise from it; not CN I or II.
Myelencephalon to medulla, metencephalon to pons, mesencephalon to midbrain.
Cerebellar peduncles: superior to midbrain, middle to pons, inferior to medulla.
Midbrain: smallest, 2 cm; tectum with four colliculi; peduncles with CN III between them.
CN IV is the only nerve emerging dorsally.
Pons: largest; basilar artery in the basilar groove; CN V to VIII.
Facial colliculus: facial fibres looping around the abducens nucleus.
Cerebellopontine angle: CN VII and VIII beside the foramen of Luschka.
Medulla: pyramids (corticospinal), olives (inferior olivary nucleus), decussation of 75 to 90 percent of corticospinal fibres.
CN XII between pyramid and olive; CN IX, X, XI behind the olive.
Aqueduct in the midbrain; fourth ventricle floor is the rhomboid fossa; obex at its caudal tip.
Reticular formation: consciousness, sleep, breathing, heart rate, pain.
Supplied by the basilar artery and its branches.
Alternating syndrome: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia.

high_yield.html: Midbrain (mesencephalon, smallest) → pons (metencephalon, largest) → medulla (myelencephalon). The thalamus is NOT brainstem.

Nerve exits: III between the cerebral peduncles; IV dorsally below the inferior colliculi (the only dorsal one); V lateral pons; VI, VII, VIII at the pontomedullary junction (medial to lateral); XII between pyramid and olive; IX, X, XI behind the olive.
2-2-4-4: 2 nerves above the brainstem (I, II), 2 in the midbrain (III, IV), 4 in the pons (V-VIII), 4 in the medulla (IX-XII).
Cerebellar peduncles: superior → midbrain; middle → pons (largest); inferior → medulla.
Pyramids = corticospinal tracts; 75-90% decussate in the lower medulla. Olive = inferior olivary nucleus.
Facial colliculus (floor of the 4th ventricle) = facial fibres looping round the abducens nucleus. A lesion there → ipsilateral VI and VII palsy.
4th ventricle: floor = rhomboid fossa; CSF exits via Magendie (median) and Luschka (lateral). Aqueduct runs through the midbrain.
Alternating (crossed) syndrome = ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy + contralateral hemiplegia: the nerve tells you the level (III → midbrain, VI/VII → pons, XII → medulla).
Cerebellopontine angle (VII, VIII by the foramen of Luschka): an acoustic neuroma gives unilateral deafness, tinnitus, then facial and trigeminal signs.
Reticular formation: consciousness and arousal, sleep-wake, cardiovascular and respiratory centres (medulla), pain modulation. Blood supply = basilar (+ vertebral) system.

deeper.title: Why an alternating syndrome points to one level
deeper.html:
A cranial nerve leaves the brainstem on its own side, while the corticospinal fibres running past it have not yet crossed, doing so in the lower medulla. A single small lesion therefore hits the cranial nerve on one side and the motor tract heading for the opposite limbs. The cranial nerve involved tells you the level: CN III for the midbrain, CN VI or VII for the pons, CN XII for the medulla.

Source: the lecture's alternating syndrome slide, read with its cranial nerve emergence table.

deeper.title: Why brainstem lesions are so dangerous
deeper.html:
Everything is packed into a few centimetres: every tract between brain and body, the nuclei of ten cranial nerves, and the reticular formation keeping you awake and breathing. A small stroke or a raised pressure pushing the brainstem down through the foramen magnum can stop breathing or consciousness outright, which is why the brainstem is called a vital centre.

Source: the lecture's functions slide and its take-home messages.

deeper.title: Why CN IV is so easily injured
deeper.html:
The trochlear nerve is the only one emerging from the back of the brainstem, the thinnest cranial nerve, and it has the longest course inside the skull as it wraps around the midbrain. That long exposed path is why it is often damaged in head injury, causing vertical double vision that the patient compensates for by tilting the head.

Source: the lecture's note that CN IV is the only nerve emerging dorsally.

deeper.title: Why a tumour at the cerebellopontine angle causes deafness first
deeper.html:
CN VII and VIII emerge side by side at the cerebellopontine angle. A tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve sheath grows there and presses on CN VIII first, causing one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus, then later on CN VII and even CN V. The lecture's description of the angle is exactly why these tumours present the way they do.

Source: the lecture's cerebellopontine angle slide.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cerebellum: posterior cranial fossa, under the tentorium, behind pons and medulla, separated by the fourth ventricle.
Role: automatic regulation of movement: muscle tone, balance, coordination. It does not start movement.
Two hemispheres + vermis. Vermis: axial muscles, posture, gait. Hemispheres: limb coordination.
Primary fissure: anterior / posterior lobes. Posterolateral fissure: posterior / flocculonodular lobes. Horizontal fissure (Vicq d'Azyr): superior / inferior surfaces.
Flocculonodular lobe = archicerebellum = vestibulocerebellum: balance and eye movements.
Tonsils: medial inferior hemispheres beside the inferior vermis; herniation compresses the medulla (respiratory and cardiovascular centres).
Peduncles: superior → midbrain (output to red nucleus and thalamus); middle → pons (largest, input from contralateral pontine nuclei); inferior → medulla (input and output).
Arbor vitae: branching white matter surrounded by grey cortex.
Cortex layers, outside in: molecular (stellate, basket), Purkinje (only output, inhibitory), granular (granule, Golgi).
Deep nuclei, lateral to medial: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial. Emboliform + globose = interposed.
Mossy fibres: spinal cord, vestibular and pontine nuclei → granule cells. Climbing fibres: contralateral inferior olive → one Purkinje cell; motor learning and errors.
Arteries: SCA and AICA from the basilar; PICA from the vertebral. Veins → superior petrosal, transverse and straight sinuses.
Spinocerebellum: vermis + intermediate zones → fastigial and interposed nuclei; tone, posture, trunk and limb coordination.
Cerebrocerebellum: lateral hemispheres → dentate → thalamus → motor cortex; planning and timing of skilled movement.
Signs are ipsilateral to the lesion.

high_yield.html: Location: posterior cranial fossa, under the tentorium, behind the pons and medulla, separated by the fourth ventricle.
Fissures: primary (anterior / posterior lobes), posterolateral (posterior / flocculonodular lobes), horizontal of Vicq d'Azyr (superior / inferior surfaces).
Deep nuclei lateral to medial: Don't Eat Greasy Food: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial.

Purkinje cells are the only output of the cortex and are inhibitory. Climbing fibres: contralateral inferior olive only. Mossy fibres: spinal cord, vestibular and pontine nuclei, ending on granule cells.
Peduncles: Superior Sends out (midbrain: red nucleus, thalamus); Middle is Massive input (pons); Inferior is In and out (medulla).
Arteries: SCA and AICA from the basilar; PICA from the vertebral.
Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral. Flocculonodular lesion: loss of equilibrium; lateral lesion: errors in skilled movements; midline lesion: trunk and gait.
Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla: a threat to breathing and circulation.

deeper.title: Why cerebellar signs are on the same side
deeper.html:
The output of a cerebellar hemisphere leaves through the superior peduncle and crosses to the opposite red nucleus and thalamus, which drive the opposite motor cortex. The corticospinal tract then crosses back in the medulla. Two crossings cancel out, so each hemisphere ends up controlling the limbs on its own side. That is why a right cerebellar lesion makes the right arm clumsy, while a right motor cortex lesion weakens the left side.

Source: the lecture's clinical significance slide; StatPearls, Neuroanatomy, Cerebellum.

deeper.title: What cerebellar signs look like at the bedside
deeper.html:
A cerebellar patient is not weak: the problem is coordination. Look for dysmetria (overshooting the target in the finger-to-nose test), intention tremor (tremor that grows as the finger approaches the target), dysdiadochokinesia (clumsy rapid alternating movements), a wide-based, unsteady gait and nystagmus. Midline (vermis) lesions mainly disturb the trunk and gait; hemisphere lesions mainly disturb the limbs on the same side.

Sources: StatPearls, Neuroanatomy, Cerebellum; TeachMeAnatomy, The Cerebellum.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Fliyou's lecture: the situation and morphology of the cerebrum, its sulci, lobes and gyri, the commissures, the grey and white matter, the basal ganglia, the functions of each lobe, the pyramidal tract, language and clinical aspects. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cerebrum = hemispheres + diencephalon.
Falx cerebri separates the hemispheres; tentorium separates cerebrum from cerebellum; fissure of Bichat from the brainstem.
Weight 1200 to 1400 g.
Central sulcus (Rolando): frontal from parietal. Lateral sulcus (Sylvius): temporal below. Calcarine fissure: medial occipital.
Insula lies deep in the lateral sulcus.
Frontal lobe: 40 percent, precentral motor gyrus. Parietal: postcentral sensory gyrus.
Wernicke's area: posterior superior temporal; Broca's: inferior frontal.
Cuneus: sixth occipital gyrus. Uncus: hooked end of the hippocampal gyrus.
Corpus callosum: 200 million fibres, genu and rostrum in front, splenium behind.
Fornix: anterior columns to mammillary bodies, posterior to hippocampus.
Internal capsule: between thalamus and caudate medially, lentiform laterally.
Lentiform = putamen + globus pallidus. Striatum = caudate + putamen.
Basal ganglia need dopamine; the subthalamic nucleus is a Parkinson's target.
Left hemisphere dominant for language in about 92 percent.
Corticospinal fibres mostly cross in the medulla.

high_yield.html: Central sulcus (Rolando): frontal vs parietal. Lateral sulcus (Sylvius): temporal below, insula hidden inside. Calcarine sulcus: primary visual cortex.

Precentral gyrus = primary motor (area 4); postcentral = primary sensory. Broca = inferior frontal gyrus (speech production); Wernicke = posterior superior temporal (comprehension), dominant (usually left) hemisphere.
Broca aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech, comprehension intact. Wernicke aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension.
Internal capsule lies between thalamus + caudate (medial) and lentiform nucleus (lateral). Lentiform = putamen + globus pallidus; striatum = caudate + putamen.
A small internal capsule stroke (lenticulostriate arteries) gives a dense contralateral hemiplegia of face, arm and leg because the fibres are packed tightly there.
Corpus callosum: rostrum, genu, body, splenium; ~200 million fibres. Fornix: hippocampus → mammillary bodies (memory circuit).
Falx cerebri separates the hemispheres; tentorium cerebelli separates cerebrum from cerebellum (supra- vs infratentorial). The foramen of Monro joins lateral and third ventricles.
Basal ganglia need dopamine from the substantia nigra: loss → Parkinson's disease (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia); the subthalamic nucleus is a deep brain stimulation target.
Lobe functions: frontal = personality, planning, motor, Broca; parietal = sensation, spatial sense; temporal = hearing, memory, Wernicke; occipital = vision; insula = taste and visceral sensation.

deeper.title: Why a small stroke in the internal capsule is so disabling
deeper.html:
The corticospinal fibres from the whole motor strip fan out over the cortex but squeeze together through the narrow internal capsule. A tiny stroke there, which in the cortex would affect only a hand or a face, can paralyse the whole opposite side at once. The lecture's capsule table is exactly why a small deep stroke causes such a large deficit.

Source: the lecture's internal capsule description and its pyramidal tract slide.

deeper.title: Why Parkinson's disease is a basal ganglia disease
deeper.html:
The lecture stresses that the basal ganglia need dopamine released by the substantia nigra. When those dopamine neurons die, the circuit that fine-tunes movement fails, giving slowness, stiffness and tremor. That is why treatment replaces dopamine, and why stimulating the subthalamic nucleus, another node in the same loop, can restore movement.

Source: the lecture's basal ganglia, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra slides.

deeper.title: Why Broca and Wernicke aphasias sound so different
deeper.html:
Broca's area in the frontal lobe produces speech, so damage leaves the patient understanding well but speaking in slow, broken words. Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe understands language, so damage leaves fluent speech that makes little sense, and the patient cannot follow what is said. Knowing which area is where lets you locate the lesion from the way a patient speaks.

Source: the lecture's language anatomy and lobe function slides.

deeper.title: Why a right-sided stroke weakens the left side
deeper.html:
Each hemisphere controls the opposite side because the corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla. A stroke above that crossing, in the cortex or internal capsule, therefore weakens the opposite limbs. The lecture's line that a right-sided stroke weakens the left arm or leg follows directly from where the tract decussates.

Source: the lecture's functional anatomy and pyramidal tract slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Fliyou's lecture: the pyramidal tracts with the corticospinal and corticobulbar pathways, the motor cortex, the extrapyramidal system and its five tracts, the lower motor neurons, the neurotransmitters of the extrapyramidal system and their clinical correlations. The lecture's review slides on the basal ganglia, diencephalon and brainstem are covered in those lectures' own pages. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pyramidal: voluntary; extrapyramidal: tone, balance, posture, locomotion.
Pyramidal pathway: two neurons, upper (cortex) and lower (ventral horn or brainstem nucleus).
Named after the medullary pyramids.
Primary motor cortex: precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4; Betz cells in layer V.
Motor area size follows precision, not muscle size: hand and tongue largest.
Corticospinal: posterior limb of the internal capsule, middle of the peduncle, pons, pyramid.
About 90 percent cross in the lower medulla (lateral CST, limbs); anterior CST stays ipsilateral (trunk).
Corticobulbar (geniculate) tract passes through the genu; ends in III, IV, VI and V, VII, IX, X, XI.
Five extrapyramidal tracts; only rubrospinal and tectospinal cross.
Vestibulospinal: anti-gravity muscles. Medial reticulospinal facilitates; lateral inhibits.
Alpha motor neurons: skeletal muscle. Gamma: muscle spindles. Medial for proximal, lateral for distal.
Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta; deficiency gives Parkinson's triad.

high_yield.html: Pyramidal = 2 neurons: upper motor neuron (Betz cells, layer V of area 4) → lower motor neuron (ventral horn or cranial nerve motor nucleus).

Corticospinal route: precentral gyrus → posterior limb of the internal capsule → middle of the cerebral peduncle → pons → pyramid → ~90% cross in the lower medulla (lateral CST, limbs); the rest stay ipsilateral (anterior CST, trunk).
Corticobulbar fibres pass through the genu of the internal capsule (not the posterior limb) and cross gradually to the cranial nerve nuclei.
Homunculus: area size follows precision, not muscle bulk → hand, face and tongue are huge.

Extrapyramidal tracts: vestibulospinal (anti-gravity: arm flexors, leg extensors), reticulospinal (medial facilitates, lateral inhibits), rubrospinal and tectospinal. Only rubrospinal and tectospinal cross.
UMN vs LMN: UMN lesion = weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, little wasting. LMN lesion = weakness, flaccidity, hyporeflexia, wasting, fasciculations.
A lesion above the decussation (cortex, capsule, brainstem) weakens the opposite side; a lesion in the cord weakens the same side below the level.
Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta smooths movement; its loss (Parkinson's) leaves relative acetylcholine excess → tremor and rigidity; anticholinergics help.
Alpha motor neurons → skeletal muscle; gamma → muscle spindles. Medial ventral horn = proximal/axial muscles; lateral = distal limb muscles.

deeper.title: Upper versus lower motor neuron lesions
deeper.html:
The two-neuron structure of the pyramidal pathway gives the most useful bedside distinction in neurology. Damage to the upper neuron, anywhere from the cortex to the cord, removes the brain's brake on the lower neuron, so the muscle becomes stiff with brisk reflexes. Damage to the lower neuron cuts the muscle off from its nerve, so it becomes floppy, wasted and areflexic. Which pattern you see tells you which neuron is damaged.

Source: the lecture's N1 and N2 description of the pyramidal pathway.

deeper.title: Why facial weakness spares the forehead in a stroke
deeper.html:
The corticobulbar fibres cross gradually as they descend, and the part of the facial nucleus supplying the forehead receives fibres from both hemispheres. So a cortical stroke weakens the lower face on the opposite side but spares the forehead, while damage to the facial nerve itself paralyses the whole half of the face. It is a classic way to tell a stroke from a Bell's palsy.

Source: the lecture's corticobulbar tract slides on gradual crossing.

deeper.title: Why anticholinergics help Parkinson's disease
deeper.html:
The lecture frames dopamine and acetylcholine as a balance in the striatum. When the substantia nigra fails and dopamine falls, acetylcholine becomes relatively dominant, which drives the tremor and rigidity. Blocking acetylcholine tips the balance back, which is why anticholinergic drugs ease these symptoms, even though they do not replace the lost dopamine.

Source: the lecture's dopamine and acetylcholine slides.

deeper.title: Why the hand area is so big
deeper.html:
The lecture notes that cortical area follows precision, not muscle size. The hand and tongue get enormous territories in the motor strip because they perform the finest, most varied movements. It explains why a small cortical stroke can take away fine finger control while leaving the powerful thigh muscles barely affected.

Source: the lecture's corticospinal tract slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Fliyou's lecture: the four parts of the diencephalon, the thalamus with its nuclei, geniculate bodies, relations, functions and blood supply, the hypothalamus, the epithalamus with the pineal gland, and the subthalamus. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Diencephalon: epithalamus, thalamus, subthalamus, hypothalamus, around the third ventricle.
Thalami joined by the interthalamic adhesion; divided by the Y-shaped internal medullary lamina into anterior, medial and lateral parts.
Pulvinar is the posterior thalamus.
LGB relays vision to the occipital cortex; MGB relays hearing to the temporal cortex.
Thalamus: medial wall forms the side of the third ventricle; anterior pole forms the back of the foramen of Monro.
Thalamus filters all sensation except smell: the gateway to the cortex.
Thalamus supplied by the posterior cerebral artery.
Hypothalamus: floor of the third ventricle, joined to the pituitary; supraoptic, tuberal and mammillary regions; homeostasis.
Epithalamus: pineal gland (melatonin), habenula, stria medullaris.
Pineal gland sits between the superior colliculi.
Subthalamus: laterally the internal capsule; subthalamic nucleus is glutamatergic.
Subthalamic nucleus lesion causes hemiballismus; it is a deep brain stimulation target.

high_yield.html: Four parts around the third ventricle: thalamus (relay), hypothalamus (homeostasis, pituitary), epithalamus (pineal, habenula), subthalamus (motor).
Thalamus = gateway to the cortex: relays every sense except smell. LGB = vision (to occipital cortex); MGB = hearing (to temporal cortex). Mnemonic: Lateral = Light, Medial = Music.

Hypothalamus forms the floor of the third ventricle and connects to the pituitary by the infundibulum. It controls hunger, thirst, temperature, circadian rhythm, the autonomic system and the pituitary.
Pineal gland (epithalamus), between the superior colliculi: melatonin in darkness → circadian rhythm.
Subthalamic nucleus lesion → contralateral hemiballismus (wild flinging of a limb), because its excitatory (glutamate) drive to the internal pallidus, which brakes the thalamus, is lost.
A pineal tumour compresses the tectum (Parinaud syndrome: loss of upward gaze) and the aqueduct (hydrocephalus).
The thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle; the hypothalamus the floor. The pons is not part of the diencephalon. Thalamus blood = posterior cerebral artery.
Thalamic stroke: contralateral loss of all sensation and sometimes a severe burning thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy).

deeper.title: Why a thalamic stroke can cause severe pain
deeper.html:
Because the thalamus filters every sensation except smell, damage to its sensory nuclei does not just remove feeling. It can distort it, leaving numbness together with burning pain on the opposite side of the body. It follows directly from the thalamus being the relay that decides what sensory information reaches the cortex.

Source: the lecture's thalamic functions slide.

deeper.title: Why a pineal tumour can cause trouble looking up
deeper.html:
The pineal gland sits in the groove between the two superior colliculi, right above the midbrain. A tumour there presses on the superior colliculi, which control vertical gaze, and can block the cerebral aqueduct below it, causing raised pressure. That is why the lecture's note on pineal tumours matters: its position explains its symptoms.

Source: the lecture's pineal gland description and its clinical note.

deeper.title: Why hemiballismus flings the opposite arm
deeper.html:
The subthalamic nucleus acts as an accelerator for the internal globus pallidus, which is itself a brake on the thalamus. Knock out the subthalamic nucleus and the brake weakens, the thalamus is released and large, wild movements appear on the opposite side. The lecture's glutamate to GABA chain is exactly the circuit behind it.

Source: the lecture's subthalamic nucleus slide.

deeper.title: Why the hypothalamus is the master regulator
deeper.html:
The hypothalamus reaches the body two ways at once: through the autonomic nervous system and through the pituitary gland, which controls most other endocrine glands. That dual reach is why a small hypothalamic lesion can disturb temperature, appetite, thirst and hormones all together.

Source: the lecture's hypothalamus slides.

title: Anatomy of the ear, part 1: external and middle ear
subject: subj:anat3

provenance.note: Ear Anatomy part 1.pdf (Anatomy 3, ENT Anatomy, Pr Hajjij Amal, 2025/2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Pr Hajjij Amal's lecture: the external ear and canal, the middle ear and its six walls, the tympanic membrane, the ossicles, the mastoid cells, the Eustachian tube and tympanic plexus, and the physiology of the external and middle ear. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: The ear lies mostly in the petrous temporal bone: external, middle and inner parts.
Pinna fixed by its anterior third; four constant projections: helix, anthelix, tragus, antitragus; the lobe has no cartilage.
Canal: 25 mm, S-shaped; outer third cartilaginous with hair and wax glands, inner two thirds bony.
Pull the pinna up, back and out to examine the drum.
Middle ear: Eustachian tube, tympanic cavity, mastoid.
Tympanic cavity: six walls, five bony plus the eardrum.
Eardrum: three layers; pars tensa with annulus; pars flaccida lacks the fibrous layer.
Roof tegmen tympani over the middle cranial fossa; floor over the jugular bulb; anterior wall over the internal carotid.
Medial wall: facial canal prominence divides the lateral semicircular canal above from the promontory, oval and round windows below.
Posterior wall: aditus ad antrum, vertical facial canal to the stylomastoid foramen.
Stapes is the smallest ossicle, about 2 mg.
Eustachian tube: 31 to 38 mm, pressure, protection, drainage.
Tympanic plexus: Jacobson's nerve (IX), carotid sympathetics, geniculate ganglion branch.
Ossicular lever overcomes the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch.

high_yield.html: External canal: 25 mm, S-shaped; outer 1/3 cartilaginous (hair, wax), inner 2/3 bony. Pull the pinna up, back and out in adults to see the drum.

Tympanic cavity walls and their neighbours: roof (tegmen) → middle cranial fossa; floor → jugular bulb; anterior → internal carotid + auditory tube; posterior → mastoid antrum (aditus) and facial canal; medial → promontory, oval and round windows; lateral → drum.
Middle ear infection can spread: up through the tegmen → meningitis/temporal lobe abscess; back → mastoiditis; and the facial nerve in its canal on the medial/posterior wall can be paralysed.
Tympanic membrane: 3 layers (skin, fibrous, mucosa). Pars flaccida (above the lateral process of the malleus) lacks the fibrous layer. Cone of light points antero-inferiorly.
Ossicles: malleus → incus → stapes (smallest bone in the body; footplate in the oval window). The lever and area ratio overcome the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch.
Auditory (Eustachian) tube: 31-38 mm, bony posterolateral part + cartilaginous anteromedial part, opening into the nasopharynx; equalises pressure (opens on swallowing and yawning).

Children's tubes are shorter, wider and more horizontal → more otitis media. Tympanic plexus = Jacobson's nerve (IX) + carotid sympathetics; IX also carries the parotid secretomotor fibres onward (lesser petrosal).
Acoustic (stapedius) reflex damps loud sound; stapedius is supplied by VII, so facial palsy can cause hyperacusis. Tensor tympani = V3.

deeper.title: Why middle ear infection can reach the brain
deeper.html:
Every wall of the tympanic cavity is thin bone with something important behind it: the middle cranial fossa above, the jugular bulb below, the internal carotid in front and the mastoid behind. That is why an untreated middle ear infection can spread to cause mastoiditis, meningitis or a temporal lobe abscess, and why the lecture lists each wall's neighbour.

Source: the lecture's six walls and their relations.

deeper.title: Why facial palsy can follow ear disease
deeper.html:
The facial nerve runs through the medial wall, then down the posterior wall to the stylomastoid foramen. Infection, a cholesteatoma or surgery in the middle ear can damage it, which is why a facial palsy on the side of an ear problem is taken seriously.

Source: the lecture's medial and posterior wall slides.

deeper.title: Why children get ear infections more
deeper.html:
The Eustachian tube drains and ventilates the middle ear. In children it is shorter, wider and more horizontal, so it drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal infection climb up. That is why otitis media and glue ear are so common in young children.

Source: the lecture's Eustachian tube slides.

deeper.title: Why the pars flaccida is a warning site
deeper.html:
Without a fibrous layer, the pars flaccida is floppy. When tube dysfunction leaves negative pressure in the middle ear, it is the part sucked inwards, forming a retraction pocket where skin debris accumulates. That is the classic origin of a cholesteatoma.

Source: the lecture's description of the pars flaccida.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Pr Hajjij Amal's lecture: the bony and membranous labyrinths, the cochlea, vestibule and semicircular canals, the organ of Corti and its hair cells, the central auditory and vestibular pathways, the vestibulocochlear nerve and the blood supply. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Bony labyrinth (cochlea, vestibule, canals) holds perilymph; membranous labyrinth (cochlear duct, utricle, saccule, ducts) holds endolymph.
Anterior labyrinth hears; posterior labyrinth balances.
Cochlea: 30 mm tube around the modiolus, two and three quarter turns; basal turn forms the promontory.
Spiral lamina divides scala vestibuli above from scala tympani below; they meet at the helicotrema.
Round window: secondary tympanic membrane. Oval window: stapes footplate and annular ligament.
Aqueduct of the cochlea joins perilymph to CSF.
Three canals at 90 degrees; lateral canal horizontal; five openings because of the crus commune.
Ductus reuniens joins cochlear duct to saccule; utriculo-saccular duct gives the endolymphatic duct and sac.
Organ of Corti hears; maculae detect static balance; cristae detect kinetic balance.
Inner hair cells carry 90 to 95 percent of the cochlear nerve fibres; outer hair cells sharpen tuning.
CN VIII divides in the internal auditory canal into cochlear and vestibular nerves.
Superior vestibular nerve: utricle, superior and lateral ampullae. Inferior: saccule.
Labyrinthine artery from the AICA or the basilar trunk.
Auditory pathway ends in the transverse temporal gyrus, mainly contralateral.

high_yield.html: Bony labyrinth (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals) contains perilymph; membranous labyrinth (cochlear duct, utricle, saccule, ducts) contains endolymph.
Front hears, back balances: cochlear duct → organ of Corti (hearing); utricle and saccule → maculae (static balance, linear acceleration); ampullae → cristae (kinetic balance, rotation).
Cochlea: 2¾ turns around the modiolus; scala vestibuli (from the oval window) and scala tympani (to the round window) meet at the helicotrema; the cochlear duct (scala media) lies between them.
Oval window = stapes footplate (into scala vestibuli). Round window = secondary tympanic membrane (end of scala tympani). The basal turn forms the promontory on the medial wall of the middle ear.
Tonotopy: high frequencies peak at the base (narrow, stiff basilar membrane), low frequencies at the apex.
Inner hair cells carry 90-95% of afferent fibres (true receptors); outer hair cells are contractile amplifiers that sharpen tuning.

Three semicircular canals at right angles open into the vestibule by 5 openings (anterior and posterior share the crus commune). Nerves: superior vestibular = utricle + anterior and lateral ampullae; inferior = saccule + posterior ampulla.

Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate → auditory cortex (transverse temporal gyri of Heschl). Bilateral, mainly contralateral.

Because the pathway is bilateral above the cochlear nuclei, a unilateral cortical lesion does not cause deafness in one ear; one-sided deafness points to the ear, VIII or cochlear nuclei (e.g. acoustic neuroma in the internal acoustic meatus).
Labyrinthine artery (usually from AICA) is an end artery: its occlusion gives sudden deafness and vertigo.

deeper.title: Why a stroke can cause sudden deafness and vertigo
deeper.html:
The labyrinthine artery is small and an end artery, arising from the AICA or the basilar trunk. Block it and both the cochlea and the vestibular system lose their supply together, giving sudden hearing loss and severe vertigo on one side. That combination points to a vascular cause in the posterior circulation, not a simple ear problem.

Source: the lecture's vascularization slide.

deeper.title: Why loud noise damages high frequencies first
deeper.html:
The travelling wave peaks at different points along the basilar membrane depending on frequency, with high frequencies near the base by the oval window. Every sound passes through the base on its way up, so those hair cells take the most wear. That is why noise-induced and age-related hearing loss start in the high frequencies.

Source: the lecture's travelling wave diagram.

deeper.title: Why the head-shake test works
deeper.html:
The lateral canal lies horizontally and signals head rotation to the vestibular nuclei, which link through the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the eye-muscle nuclei. That reflex keeps the eyes fixed on a target while the head turns. Testing it at the bedside checks the whole loop, from canal to nerve to brainstem to eye muscles.

Source: the lecture's central vestibular connections slides.

deeper.title: Why the perilymph-CSF connection matters
deeper.html:
The aqueduct of the cochlea joins the perilymph to the cerebrospinal fluid. It explains why raised intracranial pressure or infection in the subarachnoid space can affect the inner ear, and why meningitis is a leading cause of acquired deafness in children.

Source: the lecture's slide on the aqueduct of the cochlea.

title: Motor and sensory innervation of the eye and its appendages
subject: subj:anat3

provenance.note: 5. The Motor and Sensory innervation of the Eye and its appendages.pdf (Facio-Maxillary Module, Dr Zehra Jamil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the cranial nerves of the eye, the optic nerve and visual pathway, the motor nerves and their palsies, accommodation, the pupillary light reflex, the corneal reflex, and the autonomic control of the lacrimal gland. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: 128 sensory, 346/11/12 motor, 5-7-9-10 mixed; parasympathetic in 3, 7, 9, 10.
The optic nerve is wrapped in meninges with CSF around it.
Visual pathway orders: photoreceptors, bipolar cells, then the geniculate to cortex neuron.
Abducens nucleus: motor neurons for the ipsilateral lateral rectus plus interneurons crossing to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus.
MLF produces conjugate eye movement and coordinates eyes with head rotation.
Accommodation: ciliary muscle contracts, suspensory ligament relaxes, lens more convex, dioptric power increases.
Far vision at rest: ciliary muscle relaxed, ligaments taut, lens flat.
Near response: accommodation, pupil change, convergence.
Accommodation reflex afferent: retina to visual cortex. Efferent: oculomotor nucleus, ciliary ganglion, ciliary muscle.
Light reflex afferent: retina, optic nerve, chiasm, tract, pretectal nuclei, both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
Light reflex efferent: CN III, ciliary ganglion, short ciliary nerves, sphincter pupillae.
Bilateral projections give the direct and consensual responses; darkness inhibits the reflex, giving dilation.
Corneal reflex: afferent V1 to the spinal nucleus of V; efferent facial motor nucleus both sides, CN VII, orbicularis oculi.
Lacrimal gland: parasympathetic through the greater superficial petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion stimulates; sympathetic through the deep petrosal nerve inhibits.
Ciliary ganglion: parasympathetic synapse, sympathetic and sensory pass through; branches are the short ciliary nerves.
Photopic (cones): bright light, colour, detail, low light sensitivity. Scotopic (rods): dim light, no colour, high light sensitivity.

high_yield.html: Cranial nerve types: sensory 1, 2, 8; motor 3, 4, 6, 11, 12; mixed 5, 7, 9, 10; parasympathetic 3, 7, 9, 10 ('1973').
Light reflex: afferent = CN II → pretectal nuclei → both Edinger-Westphal nuclei; efferent = CN III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae. Direct + consensual.

Accommodation reflex (near triad): lens thickens + pupil constricts + convergence. Afferent goes all the way to the visual cortex; efferent = CN III (parasympathetic to ciliary and sphincter muscles, somatic to medial recti).
Corneal reflex: afferent V1 (nasociliary) → spinal nucleus of V → both facial nuclei → efferent CN VII → orbicularis oculi. Touch one cornea → both eyes blink.

In the corneal reflex, the side that fails to blink tells you which nerve is hit: no blink on either side when one cornea is touched = that side's V1; only one eye fails to blink whichever side is touched = that side's VII.
Ciliary ganglion: only the parasympathetic fibres (from CN III) synapse there; sympathetic and sensory fibres just pass through. Its output = short ciliary nerves.
Abducens nucleus has motor neurons (ipsilateral LR) and interneurons crossing in the MLF to the opposite CN III nucleus (contralateral MR): this produces conjugate horizontal gaze.

MLF lesion = internuclear ophthalmoplegia: on attempted lateral gaze, the eye on the lesion side fails to adduct and the other eye shows nystagmus; convergence is preserved. Classic in young adults with multiple sclerosis.
Relative afferent pupillary defect (swinging-light test): swinging the light to the eye with a damaged optic nerve makes both pupils dilate, because less light signal gets in.

deeper.title: Why papilloedema is visible in the eye
deeper.html:
The lecture's slide showing CSF around the optic nerve explains a classic sign. Because the subarachnoid space continues along the nerve right up to the eyeball, a rise in intracranial pressure is transmitted down that sleeve and pushes the optic disc forward. That swelling, papilloedema, is visible with an ophthalmoscope, which is why doctors look in the eye when they suspect raised pressure in the skull.

Source: the lecture's own diagram of the meningeal sheaths and CSF, read with the visual pathway slides.

deeper.title: Why the light reflex tests two different nerves
deeper.html:
The afferent limb is CN II and the efferent limb is CN III, so comparing the direct and consensual responses localises the fault. If the optic nerve of one eye is damaged, light in that eye constricts neither pupil, but light in the good eye still constricts both. If CN III is damaged, the affected pupil will not constrict to light in either eye, while the other pupil still does.

Source: the lecture's afferent and efferent pathway key, applied to its direct and consensual definitions.

deeper.title: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the MLF in practice
deeper.html:
The crossing interneurons of the abducens nucleus and the MLF are what let both eyes look sideways together. Cut the MLF between the two, and on looking to one side the abducting eye still moves while the adducting eye lags behind, even though the medial rectus works normally for convergence. This dissociation is a well-known sign of a brainstem lesion, and the lecture's abducens slide is exactly the anatomy behind it.

Source: the lecture's abducens nucleus and MLF slides.

deeper.title: Crocodile tears
deeper.html:
The parasympathetic fibres for tears and those for saliva both leave the facial nerve near the geniculate ganglion. If the nerve is injured and the fibres regrow along the wrong branch, salivary fibres can end up in the lacrimal gland. The person then produces tears when they eat rather than saliva. It is a direct consequence of the shared route shown on the lecture's lacrimal gland slide.

Source: the lecture's autonomic control of the lacrimal gland diagram.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: Tenon's capsule, the three layers of the eyeball, the aqueous fluid and intraocular pressure, the refractive media, and the retina with its photoreceptors. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Tenon's capsule runs from the optic nerve to the corneal limbus and separates the eye from orbital fat.
Cornea = one sixth of the outer coat; sclera = five sixths.
Cornea: completely avascular, highly sensitive (V1), nourished by the lacrimal gland and aqueous humour.
Episclera is the outermost layer of the sclera and attaches to Tenon's capsule.
Uvea = iris + ciliary body + choroid. Anterior: iris and ciliary body. Posterior: choroid.
Ciliary body alters lens shape (accommodation); ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour.
Miosis: light and parasympathetic, sphincter pupillae. Mydriasis: darkness and sympathetic, dilator pupillae.
Aqueous is a clear plasma-derived ultrafiltrate formed by diffusion, ultrafiltration and active secretion.
Aqueous path: ciliary body, posterior chamber, pupil, anterior chamber, then trabecular meshwork or uveoscleral route.
Trabecular route: through Schlemm's canal; 50 to 75 percent of outflow; pressure sensitive.
Uveoscleral route: through the ciliary muscle; pressure independent.
Refractive media in order: cornea, aqueous humour, lens, vitreous humour. Maximum refraction is at the cornea.
Accommodation: CN III, ciliary muscle contracts, zonules relax, lens thickens, near vision.
Lens histology: capsule, subcapsular epithelium (anterior only), lens fibres with crystallins.
Vitreous body fills about 80 percent of the posterior segment; transmits light and holds the retina and lens in place.
Optic disc = blind spot, no photoreceptors. Macula = cones for acuity, no blood vessels. Fovea = centre of macula, only cones.
Rods: about 120 million, scotopic, rhodopsin. Cones: about 6 million, photopic, iodopsin in three types.
Photoreceptors and bipolar cells make graded potentials; ganglion cells make action potentials forming the optic nerve.

high_yield.html: Three coats: fibrous (cornea 1/6 + sclera 5/6), vascular = uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid), neural (retina).
Cornea: avascular, highly sensitive (V1), fed by tears and aqueous. It does the most refraction, more than the lens.

Aqueous pathway: ciliary processes → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → angle → trabecular meshwork → Schlemm's canal (50-75%, pressure-sensitive) or uveoscleral route (pressure-independent).
Refractive media, in order: cornea → aqueous → lens → vitreous.
Accommodation (near): CN III parasympathetic → ciliary muscle contracts → zonules slacken → lens rounds up (thicker, more power). Far vision = ciliary muscle relaxed, zonules taut, lens flat.
Contracting the ciliary muscle makes the zonules relax, not tighten. Most students get the direction backwards.

Retina landmarks: optic disc = blind spot (no photoreceptors); macula = cones, no vessels; fovea = only cones, sharpest vision. Rods ≈ 120 million (dim light, rhodopsin); cones ≈ 6 million (colour, 3 types).
Photoreceptors and bipolar cells make graded potentials; only ganglion cells fire action potentials, and their axons form the optic nerve.
Glaucoma = outflow failure → raised pressure → optic nerve damage. Cataract = cloudy lens. Presbyopia = stiff lens with age, loss of near accommodation. Scleral icterus = jaundice seen in the sclera.
Miosis = sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, CN III); mydriasis = dilator pupillae (sympathetic). Anticholinergic drops dilate; they can precipitate angle-closure glaucoma.

deeper.title: Why the retina is built back to front
deeper.html:
Light has to pass through the ganglion cells and bipolar cells before it reaches the rods and cones, which sit at the back against the pigmented layer. The fovea gets around this by pushing the overlying layers aside, so light hits its cones almost directly. That is one reason foveal vision is the sharpest part of your visual field, and why you move your eyes to put what matters at its centre.

Source: lecture slides on the neural layer, read together with the retinal layer diagrams.

deeper.title: Glaucoma is a drainage problem, not a production problem
deeper.html:
The eye keeps making aqueous at a fairly steady rate whatever the pressure, because active secretion across the ciliary epithelium is pressure independent. So when pressure rises, the fault is almost always on the way out: a clogged trabecular meshwork or a blocked anterior chamber angle. It also explains the two main classes of drug: those that cut production at the ciliary body, and those that open up outflow.

Sources: lecture slides on aqueous formation and drainage; the lecture's own glaucoma section.

deeper.title: Why the cornea must stay avascular
deeper.html:
Blood vessels scatter light, so a transparent cornea cannot have any. Instead it takes oxygen and nutrients from the tear film in front and the aqueous humour behind, and keeps its collagen fibres in a precise lattice with a controlled water content. When that hydration control fails, the cornea clouds. This is also why corneal grafts are relatively well tolerated: with no blood supply, immune cells reach the graft far less easily.

Source: the lecture's cornea versus sclera comparison and its notes on hydration.

deeper.title: Presbyopia: the same change as cataract, earlier
deeper.html:
The lecture notes that lens thickness increases with age and elasticity is lost as the lens hardens. That stiffening is presbyopia: the ciliary muscle still contracts and the zonules still relax, but the lens can no longer round up, so near vision goes first. Years later the same ageing lens proteins break down and scatter light, which is a cataract. Reading glasses in your forties and cataract surgery in your seventies are two stages of one process.

Source: lecture slides on the lens, accommodation and cataract.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Zehra Jamil’s lecture: the skull and how it sits on the neck, the cranium, the facial bones one by one, the external base of the skull and the paranasal sinuses. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: 22 skull bones = 8 cranial + 14 facial. The mandible and vomer are the two unpaired facial bones.
Cranial bones: frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, occipital, 2 parietal, 2 temporal.
Atlanto-occipital joint = nodding. Atlanto-axial joint = rotation.
Sphenoid: sella turcica on the body; foramen rotundum (V2), ovale (V3) and spinosum (middle meningeal vessels) in the greater wing; optic canal in the lesser wing.
Ethmoid: cribriform plate (olfactory nerves), crista galli (falx cerebri), perpendicular plate (nasal septum), labyrinths (air cells, lamina papyracea, superior and middle conchae).
Temporal: squamous, petrous, tympanic, mastoid, styloid. Mandibular fossa for the TMJ. Zygomatic process forms the arch.
Zygomatic bone: three processes (frontal, temporal, maxillary); articulates with frontal, sphenoid, temporal and maxilla.
Maxilla: body with the maxillary sinus plus four processes (frontal, zygomatic, alveolar, palatine). Infraorbital foramen below the orbit.
Nasal septum: perpendicular plate of the ethmoid + vomer.
Mandible: mental foramen (mental nerve), mandibular foramen (inferior alveolar nerve), coronoid vs condylar processes, mandibular notch between them.
Pterion: frontal + parietal + squamous temporal + greater wing of sphenoid; thinnest part of the skull, over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
Four paired paranasal sinuses: frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoid, maxillary (largest).
Skull base bones: frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, temporal, occipital.

high_yield.html: 22 skull bones = 8 cranial + 14 facial. Unpaired facial bones: mandible and vomer. The mandible is the only mobile skull bone.
Sphenoid foramina for the trigeminal: 'Standing Room Only': Superior orbital fissure = V1, foramen Rotundum = V2, foramen Ovale = V3. Foramen spinosum = middle meningeal artery.
Ethmoid: cribriform plate (CN I), crista galli (falx cerebri), perpendicular plate (upper septum), labyrinths with superior and middle conchae and the lamina papyracea.
The inferior nasal concha is a separate bone; superior and middle conchae belong to the ethmoid. Bony septum = perpendicular plate of ethmoid + vomer.

Cranial fossae: anterior (cribriform); middle (optic canal, SOF, rotundum, ovale, spinosum, lacerum, carotid canal); posterior (internal acoustic meatus, jugular foramen, hypoglossal canal, foramen magnum).

Pterion (frontal + parietal + temporal + greater wing of sphenoid) is the thinnest spot, over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery → blow to the temple → extradural haematoma (lucid interval).
Mandible: mandibular foramen (inner ramus) = inferior alveolar nerve (dental block site); mental foramen (below premolars) = mental nerve. Coronoid process = temporalis; condylar process = TMJ.
Sinus drainage: frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid → middle meatus; posterior ethmoid → superior meatus; sphenoid → sphenoethmoidal recess. The maxillary sinus is the largest.
The maxillary sinus ostium is high on its medial wall, so it drains poorly (sinusitis); its floor lies near the upper molar roots (toothache ↔ sinus pain).
Atlanto-occipital = 'yes' (nodding); atlanto-axial = 'no' (rotation).

deeper.title: Why the sphenoid is called the keystone of the skull base
deeper.html:
The sphenoid sits in the centre of the skull base and touches almost every other skull bone (the exceptions are the nasal, lacrimal and mandible). It works as a cornerstone that spreads mechanical forces across the skull. It is also a crossroads for nerves and vessels going between the skull and the neck and face.

Sources: Anatomy Standard, Os sphenoidale; Kenhub, The sphenoid bone.

deeper.title: The three cranial fossae: a step-by-step view
deeper.html:
Looking down into the skull, the floor drops in three steps. The anterior fossa (frontal lobes) is formed by the frontal, ethmoid and sphenoid. The middle fossa (temporal lobes) is formed by the sphenoid and temporal bones, and holds most of the openings for the eye and jaw nerves. The posterior fossa (cerebellum) is formed by the temporal and occipital bones and holds the foramen magnum.

Sources: Neurosurgical Atlas, Internal skull base anatomy; DocCheck Flexikon, Skull base.

deeper.title: Sinus drainage: why sinus infections spread
deeper.html:
All the sinuses drain back into the nose. The middle meatus receives the frontal, anterior ethmoid and maxillary sinuses, all close together near the hiatus semilunaris. Because the frontal sinus drains just above the maxillary opening, fluid from the frontal sinus can run into the maxillary sinus. That is one route by which infection can spread between sinuses.

Sources: TeachMeAnatomy, Paranasal sinuses; StatPearls, Anatomy, Head and Neck, Sinuses.

deeper.title: Why the ethmoid is counted as both a cranial and a facial bone
deeper.html:
The ethmoid is a cranial bone, but only its cribriform plate contributes to the neurocranium. The rest of it (labyrinths and perpendicular plate) sits in the face, part of the nose and orbit. That is why some sources talk about 14 facial bones and others about 15 if the ethmoid is included.

Source: Elsevier Anatomy, Ethmoid bone.

deeper.title: The mandibular canal
deeper.html:
The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen and runs forward through the mandibular canal, supplying sensation to the lower teeth. Near the front it divides into its terminal branches: the mental nerve, which leaves through the mental foramen, and the incisive nerve.

Sources: Radiopaedia, Mandible; MDWiki, Dentary.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the facial muscles group by group, the branches of the facial nerve, the muscles of mastication and the temporomandibular joint. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Facial expression = CN VII. Mastication = V3. Levator palpebrae superioris is the odd one out: CN III.
Facial muscles are subcutaneous, arise from bone or fascia and insert into skin.
Occipitofrontalis: two bellies joined by the galea aponeurotica; the frontal belly has no bony attachment.
Orbicularis oculi: palpebral part closes the lids gently and involuntarily; orbital part closes them forcefully and is voluntary.
Corrugator supercilii is the frowning muscle; procerus makes transverse wrinkles over the bridge of the nose; mentalis is the pouting muscle.
Buccinator: from the maxilla, mandible and pterygomandibular raphe; keeps food between the teeth, blows air out, used in suckling.
Facial nerve branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical (the cervical branch supplies the platysma).
Four muscles of mastication: temporalis, masseter, lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid.
Temporalis inserts on the coronoid process; masseter on the angle; lateral pterygoid on the neck and disc; medial pterygoid on the medial surface of the ramus.
TMJ: articular disc, two synovial cavities, fibrocartilage-covered surfaces.
TMJ ligaments: lateral (prevents posterior dislocation), sphenomandibular, stylomandibular.
Upper part of the TMJ: protrusion and retraction. Lower part: elevation and depression, depression mostly by gravity.
In TMJ dislocation the mandibular head moves anteriorly and the patient cannot close the mouth.

high_yield.html: Facial expression = CN VII (subcutaneous, insert into skin). Mastication = V3 (attached to bone). Levator palpebrae = CN III, the odd one out.
Facial nerve branches: 'To Zanzibar By Motor Car': Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical (platysma).

Orbicularis oculi: palpebral part = gentle, involuntary blink; orbital part = forced, voluntary closure. Orbicularis oris closes the lips; buccinator keeps food between the teeth (cheek muscle, VII not V).
Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression (CN VII) even though it helps chewing; the buccal nerve of V3 only carries sensation from the cheek.
Muscles of mastication: temporalis (coronoid; posterior fibres retract), masseter (angle; elevates), medial pterygoid (medial ramus; elevates), lateral pterygoid (neck and disc; protrudes).

Lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that helps open the mouth (by pulling the condyle and disc forward); the other three close it. Opening is otherwise mostly gravity plus digastric and geniohyoid/mylohyoid.

TMJ: synovial joint with an articular disc making two cavities; surfaces covered by fibrocartilage. Upper cavity = gliding (protrusion/retraction); lower = hinge (elevation/depression). Lateral ligament prevents posterior dislocation.
TMJ dislocation is anterior (yawning, big bite): the condyle slips in front of the articular eminence and the mouth stays open.

Bell's palsy (lower motor neuron, CN VII): the whole half-face is paralysed, forehead included, eye won't close. Stroke (upper motor neuron): forehead is spared because the upper face gets input from both hemispheres.
Corrugator = frowning; procerus = wrinkles across the nasal bridge; mentalis = pouting; zygomaticus major = smiling; risorius = pulls the angle sideways.

deeper.title: Why facial muscles and chewing muscles have different nerves
deeper.html:
The two groups come from different pharyngeal arches in the embryo. The muscles of facial expression develop from the second arch, which is why they follow the facial nerve. The muscles of mastication develop from the first arch, which follows the trigeminal nerve, so they take V3. Knowing the arch makes the nerve impossible to forget.

Sources: TeachMeAnatomy, The facial nerve; Brainscape, Muscles of mastication (first arch).

deeper.title: Where the facial nerve splits into its five branches
deeper.html:
The facial nerve leaves the skull at the stylomastoid foramen, enters the parotid gland and forms the parotid plexus, which divides into the five terminal branches. The nerve passes through the gland but does not supply it: the parotid is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. That relationship is why parotid surgery risks facial palsy.

Source: TeachMeAnatomy, The facial nerve.

deeper.title: Why depression of the jaw needs so little muscle
deeper.html:
The lateral pterygoid is the muscle that starts opening the mouth, but most of the movement is done by gravity. The digastric, geniohyoid and mylohyoid only step in when something resists, for example when you open against a hand pushing your chin up. Elevation is the opposite: it is a powerful movement needing the temporalis, masseter and medial pterygoid together.

Sources: StatPearls, Anatomy, Head and Neck, Mastication muscles; lecture slides.

deeper.title: The parotid duct and the buccinator
deeper.html:
The parotid duct pierces the buccinator before opening into the mouth opposite the upper second molar. The muscle acts like a valve around it, so the duct does not balloon when the cheek is blown out.

Source: Brainscape, Muscles of mastication (parotid duct piercing buccinator).

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Pr Hajjij Amal's lecture: the situation and fixation of the larynx, its nine cartilages, joints and ligaments, the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles, the topographical compartments, histology, relations, blood supply and innervation, the physiology of phonation and the clinical correlations. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Nine cartilages: three unpaired (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis) and three paired (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform).
The cricoid is the only complete ring in the airway, at C6, the foundation stone of the larynx.
Larynx extends from the upper thyroid cartilage at C4 to the lower cricoid at C6; higher in children (C2 to C3).
Cricoarytenoid joint: rotation abducts and adducts; gliding opens and closes the posterior glottis.
Cricothyroid joint: tilting tenses the vocal cords.
Posterior cricoarytenoids are the only abductors: the safety muscles of the larynx.
Cricothyroid is the only muscle on the outer aspect and the only one on the external laryngeal nerve.
Transverse arytenoid is the only unpaired intrinsic muscle.
Tense: cricothyroid and vocalis. Relax: thyroarytenoid. Adduct: lateral cricoarytenoid and transverse arytenoid.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid, and sensation below the cords.
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve: sensation above the cords, piercing the thyrohyoid membrane.
Spaces: vestibule above the vestibular folds, ventricle between them and the vocal folds, infraglottic cavity below.
Epithelium is respiratory except at the vocal cords and upper half of the epiglottis: stratified squamous.
Lymphatics are absent at the vocal cords, rich supraglottically.
Unilateral recurrent nerve palsy: paramedian cord. Bilateral with external nerve: cadaveric position.
Vocal nodules form at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two thirds of the cords.
Voice parameters: frequency (Hz), intensity (dB), pitch.

high_yield.html: 9 cartilages: unpaired thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis; paired arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform. Cricoid = the only complete ring, at C6.
Posterior cricoarytenoid = the ONLY abductor ('safety muscle'): paralysis of both → airway closes.
Cricothyroid = the only muscle on the outside, the only one on the external laryngeal nerve, and the main tensor (pitch). All other intrinsic muscles = recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Sensation: above the vocal folds = internal laryngeal (pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery); below = recurrent laryngeal.
Transverse (inter)arytenoid is the only unpaired intrinsic muscle. Tensors = cricothyroid and vocalis; relaxer = thyroarytenoid; adductors = lateral cricoarytenoid, transverse arytenoid.

Unilateral recurrent laryngeal palsy (thyroidectomy, left-sided aortic or lung lesions): hoarse voice, cord paramedian. Bilateral: stridor, airway emergency. External laryngeal injury (superior thyroid artery ligation): weak, monotone voice, can't reach high notes.
The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch (long course → more often damaged by chest disease); the right loops under the subclavian artery.

Compartments: vestibule (above false cords) → ventricle → glottis (true cords) → infraglottic cavity. The glottis is the narrowest part in adults. Vocal cords have stratified squamous epithelium and no lymphatics.
No lymphatics at the cords → glottic cancer spreads late (good prognosis); supraglottic cancer spreads early. Vocal nodules sit at the junction of the anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 of the cords.
Emergency airway: cricothyroidotomy goes through the cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid and cricoid), a superficial, relatively avascular spot.

deeper.title: Why lymphatics explain laryngeal cancer staging
deeper.html:
The lecture's line that lymphatics are absent at the vocal cords has a large consequence. A tumour confined to the cord spreads late and has a good outlook, while a supraglottic tumour, in a very richly drained zone, reaches the internal jugular nodes early. That is why the three compartments of the larynx are staged separately, and why hoarseness in a smoker is investigated urgently.

Source: the lecture's lymphatic drainage slide and its topographical compartments.

deeper.title: Why the left recurrent nerve is the longer one
deeper.html:
The lecture notes that the recurrent nerve arises on the right at the base of the neck and on the left in the thorax. That is embryology: the nerve hooks under the sixth aortic arch, which on the right regresses so the nerve rides up on the subclavian artery, while on the left it stays as the ligamentum arteriosum, dragging the nerve down under the aortic arch. The long left course is why a lung or mediastinal mass can cause hoarseness.

Source: the lecture's description of the recurrent nerve origins.

deeper.title: Why the cricothyroid membrane is the emergency airway
deeper.html:
The median cricothyroid ligament sits just under the skin between two easily felt landmarks, the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid below, with no major vessels crossing it and no thyroid gland in the way. That is why an emergency airway is made there rather than through the trachea lower down, where the thyroid isthmus and vessels lie.

Source: the lecture's extrinsic ligaments and relations slides.

deeper.title: Why children choke more dangerously
deeper.html:
The lecture flags the glottis as a narrow zone in children, where obstructive oedema causes respiratory distress very rapidly. Airway resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius, so a millimetre of swelling in a small larynx cuts the airway far more than the same swelling in an adult. It is why croup and epiglottitis are emergencies in small children.

Source: the lecture's glottis space slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Pr Hajjij Amal's lecture: embryology, the descriptive anatomy of the nasal cavity and its four walls, the conchae and meatuses, the blood supply and innervation, the relations, the clinical correlations and nasal physiology. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Rhinos is Greek for nose; rhinology is the study of the nose and its diseases.
Six functions: respiration, olfaction, protection of the lower airway, air conditioning, vocal resonance, nasal reflexes.
Nasal cavities derive from the nasal placodes; the oronasal membrane initially separates nose from mouth.
Nasal septum: perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, vomer and septal cartilage.
Roof: nasal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal. Floor: palatine process of the maxilla (two thirds) plus horizontal plate of the palatine (one third).
Lateral wall: six bone pieces. Piriform aperture in front; choanae behind, separated by the vomer.
Three portions of the lateral wall: pre-turbinal, turbinal, retroturbinal.
Inferior concha is an independent bone with lacrimal, ethmoidal and maxillary processes; the supreme turbinate is inconstant.
Superior meatus: posterior ethmoidal cells, sphenoidal sinus, sphenopalatine foramen. Middle meatus: anterior ethmoidal cells, maxillary ostium, frontal sinus. Inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct.
Septal arteries: anterior and posterior ethmoidal (ophthalmic), sphenopalatine and greater palatine (maxillary), superior labial (facial).
Lateral wall quadrants: anterosuperior ethmoidal, anteroinferior facial and greater palatine, posterosuperior sphenopalatine, posteroinferior greater palatine.
Veins drain to the internal maxillary, ophthalmic and facial veins.
Innervation from V (spheno-palatine and internal nasal nerves) and I (olfactory).
Roof relations front to back: frontal sinus, anterior cerebral fossa, sphenoidal sinus.
Little's area holds Kiesselbach's plexus and is the commonest site of epistaxis.
Vidian nerve section controls excessive rhinorrhea.
Ventilatory functions: airflow control, filtration, humidification, heating. Three valves: nostril, nasal, septo-turbinal.

high_yield.html: Septum = perpendicular plate of ethmoid + vomer + septal cartilage. Floor = palatine process of maxilla (front 2/3) + horizontal plate of palatine (back 1/3).

Conchae: superior and middle belong to the ethmoid; the inferior concha is a separate bone. Meatus contents: superior = posterior ethmoid cells (+ sphenopalatine foramen); middle = frontal, maxillary, anterior ethmoid; inferior = nasolacrimal duct.
Blood supply from both carotids: ICA via ophthalmic → anterior and posterior ethmoidal; ECA via maxillary → sphenopalatine and greater palatine, and via facial → superior labial.

Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), anteroinferior septum: anterior ethmoidal + sphenopalatine + greater palatine + superior labial meet → commonest site of epistaxis (nose picking). Severe posterior bleeds come from the sphenopalatine artery.
Nerves: smell = CN I through the cribriform plate (roof, upper septum, superior concha); general sensation = V1 (anterior ethmoidal) and V2 (nasopalatine, sphenopalatine branches).
Cribriform plate fracture: CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia. Allergic rhinitis: swollen mucosa over the inferior concha; Vidian nerve section reduces severe rhinorrhoea.
Nose functions: warm, humidify, filter (mucociliary clearance), smell, resonance, reflexes. Choanae open into the nasopharynx and are separated by the vomer.
Embryology: nasal cavities come from the nasal placodes; the oronasal membrane first separates nose and mouth; the palate completes the separation. Failure = cleft palate / choanal atresia.

deeper.title: Why epistaxis has two very different patterns
deeper.html:
The lecture stresses that the nose is supplied by both carotid systems, and that split matters at the bedside. Anterior bleeds come from Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area and are usually venous or from small vessels, typical in children and stoppable by pinching the soft part of the nose. Posterior bleeds come from the sphenopalatine artery, a maxillary branch of the external carotid, and are heavier, more common in older patients and often need packing or cautery.

Source: the lecture's vascularization slides and its Little's area correlation.

deeper.title: Why the skull base is the nose's dangerous neighbour
deeper.html:
The roof of the nasal cavity is the cribriform plate, with the anterior cerebral fossa immediately above. That is why a fracture there can leak cerebrospinal fluid into the nose, and why olfactory nerve fibres passing through the plate are torn in head injury, causing loss of smell. It is also why endoscopic sinus surgery carries a small risk of entering the cranial cavity.

Source: the lecture's roof relations and its emphasis on the skull base relationship.

deeper.title: Why turbulent flow is the point, not a flaw
deeper.html:
The conchae break up the airstream on purpose. Laminar air would slip through untouched; turbulent air is thrown against the mucosa again and again, so particles stick to the mucus, water evaporates into the stream and heat transfers from the surface. The lecture's figure of about 70 percent of warming happening in the nasal cavity is the result of that design.

Source: the lecture's regulation of airflow and warming slides.

deeper.title: Why sinus disease starts at the ostium
deeper.html:
The lecture's physiology of the ostia is a small vicious circle worth memorising. Mucosal oedema narrows the ostium, drainage fails, the trapped air is absorbed and the sinus becomes hypoxic, cilia slow down, secretions thicken and more oedema follows. That is why treatment of sinusitis aims at reopening the ostium, and why surgery targets the osteomeatal complex in the middle meatus.

Source: the lecture's physiology of ostia diagram.
