title: The forgotten triangles of the neck
subject: subj:anat3

provenance.note: Forgotten triangles of neck.pdf (Singh, Vashistha, Chaudhary and Kaur, Annals of Maxillofacial Surgery, 2016)

body.build_note: Built from the assigned paper. This lecture is a published open-access article rather than a slide deck. The page follows it: the anatomic layout of the neck, the two major triangles and their subdivisions, then Farabeuf's, Lesser's, Pirogoff's and Beclard's triangles. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Sternocleidomastoid divides each side of the neck into the anterior and posterior triangles.
Anterior triangle: SCM laterally, midline medially, mandible superiorly.
Posterior triangle: SCM anteromedially, trapezius posterolaterally, clavicle inferiorly.
Anterior subdivisions: carotid, submandibular and muscular (paired) plus the submental (unpaired).
Posterior subdivisions: occipital and subclavian (omoclavicular).
Carotid triangle: omohyoid below, stylohyoid and posterior digastric above, SCM behind. It contains Farabeuf's triangle.
Farabeuf's triangle: internal jugular vein, common facial vein and hypoglossal nerve. Contents: the carotid bifurcation and the jugulodigastric node.
Submandibular triangle: divided by the stylomandibular ligament; main content the submandibular gland; external carotid in the posterior part.
Lesser's triangle: hypoglossal nerve, digastric bellies, mylohyoid. Floor: hyoglossus and mylohyoid.
Pirogoff's triangle: hypoglossal nerve, intermediate tendon of digastric, posterior border of mylohyoid. May contain the lingual artery.
Beclard's triangle: greater cornu of hyoid, posterior belly of digastric, posterior border of hyoglossus. Contains the lingual artery and hypoglossal nerve.
These triangles are landmarks for identifying the carotid, ligating the lingual artery and finding the hypoglossal nerve.

high_yield.html: SCM splits the neck: anterior triangle (SCM, midline, mandible) and posterior triangle (SCM, trapezius, clavicle).
Anterior triangle subdivisions: carotid, submandibular, muscular (paired) + submental (unpaired). Posterior: occipital and subclavian (omoclavicular).
Carotid triangle: superior belly of omohyoid, posterior belly of digastric (+ stylohyoid), SCM. Holds the carotid bifurcation, IJV and vagus.
Farabeuf's triangle: IJV (posterior), common facial vein (anteroinferior), hypoglossal nerve (superior). Contents: carotid bifurcation + jugulodigastric node. Used to find the carotid fork.

The three 'forgotten' triangles sit in the submandibular triangle and all share the hypoglossal nerve or digastric: Lesser's and Pirogoff's (XII above, digastric tendon below, mylohyoid behind) and Béclard's (greater horn of hyoid, posterior digastric, hyoglossus).
Béclard's triangle contains the lingual artery (posterior to hyoglossus) and XII; the lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus while the hypoglossal nerve lies superficial to it.
Practical uses: find the common carotid (Farabeuf), ligate the lingual artery (Béclard/Pirogoff) in tongue bleeding, and protect XII in submandibular gland surgery.

deeper.title: Why the hypoglossal nerve keeps appearing
deeper.html:
Look at the three forgotten triangles together and one structure is in all of them: the hypoglossal nerve. It forms the base of Farabeuf's triangle, the superior border of both Lesser's and Pirogoff's triangles, and it is a content of Beclard's. That is not a coincidence. The nerve runs a long, superficial course across this region on its way to the tongue, so surgeons use the triangles to find it, and use it in turn to find everything else.

Source: the paper's descriptions of all four triangles, read side by side.

deeper.title: Why you ligate the lingual artery in a triangle
deeper.html:
Beclard's triangle is called the posterior triangle of the lingual artery for a practical reason. The artery is hard to find because it dives under hyoglossus, so a surgeon needing to tie it off, for example before tongue surgery, uses the hyoid, digastric and hyoglossus as fixed walls to locate it. Pirogoff's triangle is the other approach, where the artery lies under the hyoglossus fibres.

Source: the paper's accounts of Beclard's and Pirogoff's triangles.

deeper.title: Why the deep fascia has to come off first
deeper.html:
The paper makes a point that is easy to skip: the two major triangles are covered by the deep cervical fascia, and the secondary triangles only appear once it is removed. In the dissection room that means you cannot see the carotid or submandibular triangles until you clear the investing layer. It is also why surface landmarks alone are not enough to plan a neck dissection.

Source: the paper's anatomic layout section.

deeper.title: Why these triangles were forgotten
deeper.html:
They carry surgeons' names from the nineteenth century, when anatomy was taught as a map for the hand rather than for imaging. Modern practice leans on CT and ultrasound, so eponymous triangles fell out of textbooks. The authors' argument is that they remain constant and reliable when the surgeon is looking at real tissue rather than a screen, which is exactly when landmarks matter most.

Source: the paper's introduction and conclusion.

title: Introduction and embryological development of the CNS
subject: subj:anat3

provenance.note: Introduction and embryological development of the central nervous system.pdf (Anatomy 3, Neuroanatomy lecture 1, Prof. F. Fliyou)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: CNS = brain (cerebrum, brainstem, cerebellum) + spinal cord; protected by skull, vertebral column, meninges and CSF.
PNS = 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves, and peripheral ganglia (sensory and autonomic).
Somatic system: voluntary actions. Autonomic: automatic responses; sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest).
Neuron: soma, dendrites (receive), axon (sends away), terminals (release neurotransmitters).
Myelin: oligodendrocytes in the CNS, Schwann cells in the PNS.
Astrocytes: support and blood-brain barrier. Microglia: immune cells. Ependymal cells: line ventricles, CSF.
Grey matter = cell bodies (cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus, cord centre). White matter = myelinated axons (corpus callosum, internal capsule, cord periphery).
Nervous system derives from ectoderm: neural plate → groove → tube (days 18-28).
Neuropores: anterior closes ~day 25, posterior ~day 27.
3 primary vesicles (week 4): prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon.
5 secondary vesicles (week 5): telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon.
Metencephalon → pons + cerebellum; myelencephalon → medulla; diencephalon → thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus.
Lumen of the neural tube → ventricular system: lateral (telencephalon), third (diencephalon), aqueduct (midbrain), fourth (rhombencephalon).
Flexures: cephalic (midbrain, most prominent), cervical (brain-cord, temporary), pontine (thins the 4th ventricle roof).
Neural tube defects: spina bifida (caudal), anencephaly (cranial, not survivable).

high_yield.html: CNS = brain + spinal cord. PNS = 12 cranial nerves, 31 spinal nerves, ganglia.
Myelin: oligodendrocytes (CNS), Schwann cells (PNS). Microglia: immune. Ependymal cells: CSF. Astrocytes: blood-brain barrier.
Grey matter outside in the brain (cortex), inside in the cord (butterfly). White matter = myelinated axons.
Ectoderm → neural plate → groove → tube (days 18-28). Anterior neuropore closes ~day 25, posterior ~day 27.
3 → 5: Pros → Tel + Di; Mes stays Mes; Rhomb → Met (pons, cerebellum) + Myel (medulla).
Neural tube lumen → ventricular system: lateral (tel), third (di), aqueduct (mes), fourth (rhomb).
Flexures: cephalic (midbrain, most prominent), cervical (temporary), pontine (thin 4th ventricle roof, room for the cerebellum).
Spina bifida: caudal closure failure. Anencephaly: cranial closure failure, not survivable.

deeper.title: Why folic acid matters before pregnancy
deeper.html:
The neural tube closes by about day 28, often before a woman knows she is pregnant. Folic acid taken before conception and in early pregnancy markedly lowers the risk of neural tube defects, which is why it is recommended for anyone who may become pregnant, and why some countries fortify flour with it.

Sources: WHO, Periconceptional folic acid supplementation to prevent neural tube defects; CDC, Folic acid.

deeper.title: From vesicles to ventricles: one picture to remember
deeper.html:
Think of the neural tube as a hose whose walls thicken into brain and whose inside stays open as the ventricles. Wherever a vesicle grows a lot, its cavity grows too: the huge telencephalon gives the large lateral ventricles, the thin diencephalon a slit-like third ventricle, the narrow midbrain only an aqueduct, and the rhombencephalon the fourth ventricle. This is why a block in the aqueduct swells the ventricles above it.

Source: the lecture's secondary vesicle slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the ophthalmic artery and its branches, the venous drainage of the orbit, and the clinical conditions from strabismus and nystagmus to blowout fractures, ptosis, glaucoma and retinal detachment. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. This is anatomy teaching, not clinical guidance: treatment decisions belong to your professors and to qualified clinicians.
exam_points: The ophthalmic artery is the first branch of the internal carotid and enters through the optic canal.
Orbital branches: internal palpebral, frontal, nasal, lacrimal, supraorbital, anterior and posterior ethmoidal.
Ocular branches: short ciliary (choroid, ciliary processes), long ciliary (anterior segment), central retinal (retina), muscular.
The central retinal artery enters the optic nerve sheath about 13 mm behind the globe.
Superior ophthalmic vein is the main drainage, through the superior orbital fissure to the cavernous sinus.
Vortex veins drain the uveal tract and pierce the sclera behind the equator.
Strabismus types: esotropia in, exotropia out, hypotropia down, hypertropia up.
Nystagmus: repetitive uncontrolled movements, horizontal, vertical or rotary, usually from brain injury.
Myopia: image in front of the retina. Hyperopia: image behind the retina.
Blowout fracture: the floor is most common; the medial wall second; the roof can leak CSF; the lateral wall is the strongest.
Ptosis: levator palpebrae superioris, CN III, plus the sympathetic superior tarsal muscle.
Chalazion: blocked meibomian gland inside the lid. Stye: blocked oil gland at the lid edge.
Conjunctivitis: outer layer. Uveitis: middle layer.
Papilloedema: optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure.
Glaucoma: damage to the optic nerve, open-angle slow, closed-angle sudden.
Direct reflex: same eye. Consensual reflex: opposite eye.
Absent corneal reflex: deep coma or stroke, or a trigeminal or facial nerve lesion.
Pituitary tumour at the chiasm: bitemporal hemianopia.
Ganglion cells continue as the optic nerve.

high_yield.html: Ophthalmic artery = first branch of the internal carotid, enters via the optic canal. Its central retinal artery enters the optic nerve ~13 mm behind the globe and is an end artery.
Superior ophthalmic vein (main drainage) → superior orbital fissure → cavernous sinus. Vortex veins drain the choroid.
Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye; pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea.
Danger zone: facial infection → facial/angular vein → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus thrombosis (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia of III, IV, VI, V1 numbness).
Strabismus: eso = in, exo = out, hyper = up, hypo = down. Myopia: image in front of the retina (long eye) → concave lens. Hyperopia: image behind the retina (short eye) → convex lens.
Blowout fractures: floor most common (inferior rectus trapped), then medial wall (medial rectus into ethmoid cells); roof fractures can leak CSF; the lateral wall rarely breaks.
Chalazion = blocked meibomian gland inside the lid (painless lump). Stye = infected gland at the lid margin (painful). Conjunctivitis = outer layer; uveitis = middle layer.
Pituitary tumour → bitemporal hemianopia (crossing nasal fibres carry the temporal fields). Not homonymous, not monocular.

Papilloedema = swollen optic disc from raised intracranial pressure (the optic nerve sheath continues the subarachnoid space). Retinal detachment: flashes, floaters, a curtain over vision: an emergency.
Glaucoma: open-angle = slow, painless, peripheral field loss first; closed-angle = sudden red painful eye, halos, fixed mid-dilated pupil: an emergency.

deeper.title: Why central retinal artery occlusion blinds so fast
deeper.html:
The central retinal artery is an end artery: it enters the optic nerve sheath about 13 mm behind the globe and has almost no useful collateral supply to the inner retina. Block it and the inner retina loses its blood supply at once, giving sudden painless loss of vision in that eye. It is the eye's equivalent of a stroke, and it is treated with the same urgency.

Source: the lecture's description of the central retinal artery and its course.

deeper.title: Why the floor of the orbit gives way first
deeper.html:
The lecture asks which wall is most prone to injury and which is strongest. The answer follows from the bones: the floor is thin maxillary bone sitting over the air-filled maxillary sinus, so a blow to the globe transmits pressure into the orbit and the floor buckles into the sinus below, taking fat and sometimes the inferior rectus with it. The lateral wall, of zygomatic bone and the greater wing of the sphenoid, is thick and buttressed by muscle, so it only fails in severe craniofacial trauma.

Source: the lecture's blowout fracture slides, read with the orbital wall anatomy from the first lecture.

deeper.title: Why a facial nerve palsy threatens the cornea
deeper.html:
The orbicularis oculi closes the lid, and it is supplied by CN VII. Lose that nerve and the eye cannot close fully, so the cornea dries out and loses the protective sweep of the blink. Because the corneal reflex's efferent limb is also CN VII, the reflex is lost on that side even though sensation through V1 is intact. That is why eye protection is part of managing a facial palsy.

Source: the lecture's facial nerve palsy and corneal reflex slides.

deeper.title: Why glaucoma is called the silent thief of sight
deeper.html:
The lecture notes that symptoms start so slowly they are hardly noticed. Glaucoma takes the peripheral field first, and the two eyes overlap enough that one covers the other's loss for years. Central acuity, which is what a reading chart tests, stays normal until late. That is why the lecture insists the only way to find out is a comprehensive dilated eye exam rather than waiting for symptoms.

Source: the lecture's glaucoma slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the extraocular muscles with their origins, insertions, nerves and actions, the neural layer of the retina, the visual pathway with its lesion sites, and the pupillary light reflex. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: All four recti arise from the common ring tendon; SO from the body of the sphenoid; IO from the anterior floor of the orbit.
Levator palpebrae superioris: lesser wing of the sphenoid to the superior tarsus and lid skin; CN III plus sympathetic fibres to the superior tarsal muscle.
SO tendon passes through the trochlea; it inserts deep to the superior rectus.
LR6 SO4: lateral rectus CN VI, superior oblique CN IV, all others CN III.
SR: elevation, intorsion, adduction. IR: depression, extorsion, adduction. MR: adduction. LR: abduction.
SO: intorsion, depression, abduction. IO: extorsion, elevation, abduction.
Neural layer ends at the ora serrata; the pigmented layer absorbs light to reduce scattering.
Non-visual retina covers the ciliary body and the back of the iris and is not sensitive to light.
Photoreceptors and bipolar cells: graded potentials. Ganglion cells: action potentials, forming the optic nerve.
Visual pathway: eye, optic nerve, chiasm, tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, primary visual cortex.
Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm; temporal fibres do not.
Optic nerve cut: blindness in that eye. Chiasm: loss of the temporal fields of both eyes. Tract or radiation: identical loss on one side in both eyes.
Pupillary light reflex: optic nerve, pretectum, Edinger-Westphal nucleus, CN III, ciliary ganglion, pupillary constrictor. Bilateral, so both pupils constrict.

high_yield.html: Innervation: LR6 SO4, rest 3. Recti arise from the common tendinous ring; SO from the sphenoid body (tendon through the trochlea); IO from the orbital floor.
Actions: SR = elevation, adduction, intorsion. IR = depression, adduction, extorsion. SO = depression, abduction, intorsion. IO = elevation, abduction, extorsion. MR = adduction; LR = abduction.
'Superiors intort, inferiors extort'; 'recti adduct, obliques abduct'; the obliques move the eye vertically opposite to their name (SO looks down, IO looks up).
Anatomical action ≠ clinical test position. To isolate the obliques, adduct first: SO is tested looking down and in, IO up and in. To isolate SR and IR, abduct first: SR up and out, IR down and out.
Visual pathway: retina → optic nerve → chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiation → primary visual cortex (occipital, area 17).
Lesion map: optic nerve → blind eye. Chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract or radiation → contralateral homonymous hemianopia (same half-field lost in both eyes).

CN III palsy: eye 'down and out', ptosis, dilated pupil (compressive lesions such as a posterior communicating aneurysm hit the pupil early). CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia worse looking down (stairs, reading), head tilted away from the lesion. CN VI palsy: cannot abduct, eye turns in (esotropia).

Pupillary light reflex is bilateral (pretectum → both Edinger-Westphal nuclei), so light in one eye constricts both. A blind eye from an optic nerve lesion still constricts consensually when the good eye is lit.

deeper.title: Why a pituitary tumour takes your peripheral vision
deeper.html:
The lecture's site 3 has a common clinical cause. The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica, directly beneath the optic chiasm, so a growing pituitary adenoma pushes up into the crossing fibres from the nasal halves of both retinas. Those fibres carry the temporal (outer) halves of the visual field, so the patient loses peripheral vision on both sides: bitemporal hemianopia. Patients often notice it by bumping into door frames rather than by any change in central vision.

Sources: student flashcard sets on visual pathway lesions, cross-checked against the lecture's own site diagram.

deeper.title: Why a blown pupil is an emergency sign
deeper.html:
The parasympathetic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel on the surface of the oculomotor nerve, not deep inside it. That superficial position means anything compressing the nerve from outside, such as an aneurysm or a brain herniating through the tentorium, squeezes those fibres first. So a fixed, dilated pupil can appear before any eye movement problem, which is why it is checked so urgently in head injury.

Source: Duong, Neuro-ophthalmology (review chapter on the afferent and efferent pupillary pathways).

deeper.title: The swinging torch test
deeper.html:
The bilateral wiring of the reflex gives a neat bedside test. Move a light quickly from one eye to the other. Normally both pupils stay constricted. If one optic nerve is damaged, shining the light into that eye sends a weaker signal, so both pupils paradoxically dilate when the light swings onto it: a relative afferent pupillary defect. It isolates a problem in the afferent limb, the optic nerve, from one in the efferent limb, CN III.

Source: student flashcard sets on the pupillary pathway, consistent with the lecture's reflex diagram.

deeper.title: Why the superior oblique needs a pulley
deeper.html:
The superior oblique arises at the orbital apex like the other muscles, but a muscle pulling straight back from there could only retract the eye. The trochlea solves this: the tendon hooks through it at the front of the orbit and doubles back, so the effective pull comes from in front and above. That is why a muscle arising at the back of the orbit can depress and intort the eye, and why damage to the trochlea itself can mimic a CN IV palsy.

Source: the lecture's own description of the trochlea changing the tendon's direction, read with the muscle action grid.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the oral cavity and its two parts, the floor of the mouth, the tongue with its surfaces, muscles, nerves, vessels and lymphatics, the hard and soft palate with the palatine muscles, and the three major salivary glands. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Oral cavity: lips to the oropharyngeal isthmus; vestibule plus oral cavity proper.
Vestibule: between cheeks and gums; buccinator forms its lateral wall; parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar.
Oral cavity proper: roof the hard then soft palate; floor the mylohyoid.
Sensory: roof V2 (greater palatine, nasopalatine), floor and cheek V3 (lingual, buccal). Motor to buccinator and orbicularis oris: CN VII.
Tongue: three parts, sulcus terminalis with the foramen cecum at its apex, a thyroglossal duct remnant.
Papillae: filiform, fungiform, vallate on the anterior two thirds; lingual tonsils on the posterior third.
Intrinsic muscles alter the shape; extrinsic muscles (palatoglossus, genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) move the tongue.
Protrusion: genioglossus. Retraction: styloglossus and hyoglossus. Depression: hyoglossus and genioglossus. Elevation: styloglossus and palatoglossus.
Tongue sensation: V3 lingual (general) and CN VII chorda tympani (taste) anteriorly; CN IX posteriorly; CN X at the base.
Tongue motor: CN XII for all muscles except palatoglossus, which takes CN X.
Lymph: tip to submental, anterior two thirds to submandibular, posterior third to deep cervical (jugulodigastric).
Hard palate: palatine processes of the maxillae plus horizontal plates of the palatine bones.
Palatine aponeurosis is the expanded tendon of tensor veli palatini.
Tensor veli palatini is the only palatine muscle on V3; all the others take the pharyngeal plexus.
Parotid: largest, purely serous, Stensen's duct opposite the upper second molar, CN IX via the otic ganglion.
Submandibular: second largest, mixed but serous predominates, Wharton's duct at the sublingual papilla, CN VII via the submandibular ganglion.
Sublingual: smallest, mixed but mucous predominates, ducts of Rivinus along the sublingual fold.

high_yield.html: Tongue nerves: anterior 2/3 = lingual (V3) for touch + chorda tympani (VII) for taste; posterior 1/3 = IX for both; base/epiglottis area = X (internal laryngeal).
Motor to the tongue = XII, for every muscle except palatoglossus (X). Genioglossus protrudes; styloglossus and hyoglossus retract.
Hypoglossal palsy: the protruded tongue deviates towards the paralysed side (the healthy genioglossus pushes it over).
Palate muscles: all on the pharyngeal plexus (X) except tensor veli palatini (V3). The palatine aponeurosis is the expanded tendon of tensor veli palatini.
Vagus lesion: the uvula deviates away from the paralysed side (the healthy levator pulls it over).

Salivary ducts: parotid (Stensen) opens opposite the upper 2nd molar; submandibular (Wharton) on the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum; sublingual via many small ducts (Rivinus) on the sublingual fold.
Salivary secretomotor pathways: parotid = IX → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal (V3). Submandibular and sublingual = VII → chorda tympani → lingual → submandibular ganglion.
Gland type: parotid = purely serous (largest); submandibular = mixed, mostly serous; sublingual = mixed, mostly mucous (smallest). The facial nerve passes through the parotid but does not supply it.
Foramen caecum at the apex of the sulcus terminalis = origin of the thyroglossal duct (thyroglossal cysts, lingual thyroid). Posterior third has no papillae but the lingual tonsil.
Tongue lymph: tip → submental (both sides); anterior 2/3 → submandibular; posterior 1/3 → deep cervical (jugulodigastric). Tumours near the midline can spread bilaterally.

deeper.title: Why a hypoglossal palsy makes the tongue point at the lesion
deeper.html:
The genioglossus protrudes the tongue by pulling its root forward, and each side pushes the tongue toward the opposite side. Lose one hypoglossal nerve and the healthy genioglossus is unopposed, so on protrusion the tongue deviates toward the weak side. It is a quick bedside test that follows directly from the muscle's action.

Source: the lecture's extrinsic muscle table and its protrusion line.

deeper.title: Why the tongue needs four cranial nerves
deeper.html:
The odd nerve supply is embryology showing through. The anterior two thirds come from the first pharyngeal arch, so general sensation follows V3, while taste is carried by CN VII, whose chorda tympani hitches a ride on the lingual nerve. The posterior third comes from the third arch and takes CN IX for both, and the base from the fourth arch takes CN X. The muscles come from occipital somites, which is why they follow CN XII.

Source: the lecture's sensory and motor supply slides, read with the three-part division of the tongue.

deeper.title: Why stones form in the submandibular gland
deeper.html:
Wharton's duct runs uphill: it travels forward and upward above the mylohyoid to open at the sublingual papilla, so drainage works against gravity. The submandibular saliva is also more viscous and richer in calcium than the parotid's. Those two facts together are why the great majority of salivary stones form here, classically giving pain and swelling under the jaw at mealtimes.

Source: the lecture's submandibular duct description and its mixed gland composition.

deeper.title: Why mumps hurts to chew
deeper.html:
The parotid is wrapped in a tough fascial capsule and sits between the mandible and the mastoid. When it swells, the capsule will not stretch, so pressure rises inside it, and moving the mandible presses on the gland further. The facial nerve running through the gland also explains why parotid surgery risks facial palsy, and why an enlarging parotid mass that causes facial weakness is a worrying sign.

Source: the lecture's parotid gland slide, including the facial nerve passing through it.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: orbital margins, walls, foramina and fissures, optic canal, and the muscle attachments. The wording of the slides was compared with the pictures on them, and every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. The diagrams are schematics drawn for this site. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Seven bones: 3 cranial (frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid) and 4 facial (zygomatic, lacrimal, maxilla, palatine).
Roof: frontal + lesser wing of sphenoid. Floor: maxilla + zygomatic + palatine. Medial: maxilla + lacrimal + ethmoid + sphenoid. Lateral: zygomatic + greater wing of sphenoid.
Lateral wall is the strongest. Medial wall (lamina papyracea) is the thinnest.
The floor of the orbit is the roof of the maxillary sinus.
Optic canal: optic nerve and ophthalmic artery only.
Superior orbital fissure: outside the ring = lacrimal, frontal, trochlear, superior ophthalmic vein. Inside the ring = CN III, CN VI, nasociliary.
Inferior orbital fissure: V2 branches (infraorbital, zygomatic) and infraorbital vessels.
Supraorbital notch: supraorbital nerve and vessels. Infraorbital foramen: infraorbital nerve and vessels.
Inferior oblique is the only extraocular muscle that does not arise at the apex.
LR6 SO4: lateral rectus CN VI, superior oblique CN IV, all the rest CN III.
Medial walls parallel, lateral walls about 90 degrees, orbital axes about 45 degrees, visual axes parallel.

high_yield.html: Seven bones: 3 cranial (frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid) + 4 facial (zygomatic, lacrimal, maxilla, palatine). Know which bones build each wall: roof = frontal + lesser wing; floor = maxilla + zygomatic + palatine; medial = maxilla + lacrimal + ethmoid + sphenoid; lateral = zygomatic + greater wing.
Strongest wall = lateral. Thinnest = medial (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid). Commonest blowout = floor (roof of the maxillary sinus).
Optic canal carries only two things: CN II and the ophthalmic artery. Everything else of note goes through the fissures.

Superior orbital fissure: inside the tendinous ring = CN III (both divisions), nasociliary, CN VI; outside the ring = lacrimal, frontal, CN IV, superior ophthalmic vein. Inferior orbital fissure = V2 branches (infraorbital, zygomatic) and infraorbital vessels.

LR6 SO4: lateral rectus = CN VI, superior oblique = CN IV, all other orbital muscles (including levator palpebrae) = CN III. Outside the ring, 'LFT' (lacrimal, frontal, trochlear) plus the superior ophthalmic vein.

Inferior oblique is the only extraocular muscle that does not arise at the apex: it comes from the front of the orbital floor (maxilla). The superior oblique arises from the sphenoid body, not the ring.
Orbital axis ≠ visual axis: orbital axes diverge (about 45° apart, ~22.5° each from the midline); visual axes are parallel. Medial walls are parallel; lateral walls are at about 90°.

Floor blowout: fat and inferior rectus herniate into the maxillary sinus → diplopia on upgaze, and numb cheek/upper lip from the infraorbital nerve in the floor. Ethmoid sinusitis spreads through the thin lamina papyracea → orbital cellulitis.
Superior orbital fissure syndrome: III, IV, VI and V1 hit together → ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, fixed dilated pupil and forehead numbness. Add CN II loss and it becomes an orbital apex syndrome.

deeper.title: How the tendinous ring splits the superior orbital fissure
deeper.html:
The common tendinous ring divides the fissure into three sectors: a lateral sector (lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves, and the superior ophthalmic vein), a central sector inside the ring (both divisions of CN III, the nasociliary nerve, and CN VI) and an inferior sector (inferior ophthalmic vein).

A useful way to remember the outside group is LFT: lacrimal, frontal, trochlear. That helps when you are asked which nerves lie outside the muscle cone.

Sources: EyeWiki, Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome; Neurosurgical Atlas, Superior view of contents of the left orbit.

deeper.title: Why a fissure injury shows up as an eye movement problem
deeper.html:
Because CN III, IV and VI all cross the superior orbital fissure, damage there can affect several eye movement nerves at once. In one review the abducens nerve was described as the most commonly damaged, because it lies inside the central sector close to the greater wing and has a long course.

Source: EyeWiki, Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome.

deeper.title: Orbit size in numbers
deeper.html:
The orbit holds roughly 30 mL, of which the eyeball itself takes about 7.5 mL. The long axis of the orbit measures about 44 to 50 mm. The widest diameter of the orbit is not at the rim but about 1 cm behind it, so the orbit is often compared to a pear with its stalk at the optic canal.

Source: Bertelli, Orbit chapter (Piccin, 2019, sample pages).

deeper.title: Tear drainage and the bony canal
deeper.html:
The lacrimal fossa is bounded by the anterior lacrimal crest (maxilla) and the posterior lacrimal crest (lacrimal bone). It holds the lacrimal sac and continues as the bony nasolacrimal canal, which opens into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity. That is how tears from the eye end up in the nose.

Sources: StatPearls, Anatomy, Head and Neck, Orbit; Anatomy of Orbit (drtbalu.com).

deeper.title: Trochlea: the only cartilage in the orbit
deeper.html:
The trochlea is a small pulley-like structure, attached at the trochlear fossa, through which the superior oblique tendon passes before turning to reach the eyeball. Kenhub describes it as the only cartilage found in the orbit.

Source: Kenhub, Bones of the orbit.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the contents of the orbit, the eyelids layer by layer, the conjunctiva, the tear film, the lacrimal gland and its innervation, and the ciliary ganglion. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Orbital contents: eyeball, extraocular muscles, fascia bulbi, nerves, ciliary ganglion, ophthalmic vessels, lacrimal gland, orbital fat.
Levator palpebrae superioris: CN III; its smooth part (superior tarsal muscle) is sympathetic.
Eyelid is 2 to 3 mm thick; the lateral, ciliary part carries the lashes.
Five layers: skin and cilia, loose connective and adipose tissue, muscular layer, tarsal plate, palpebral conjunctiva.
Orbital septum connects the tarsi to the orbital margins and limits the spread of infection between face and orbit.
Glands of Zeis are sebaceous; glands of Moll are modified apocrine sweat glands.
Conjunctival fornices are where palpebral becomes bulbar conjunctiva, enclosing the conjunctival sac.
Tear film: oil (meibomian), water (lacrimal), mucin (goblet cells).
Lacrimal gland sits superolaterally in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone; orbital and palpebral parts; compound tubuloacinar.
Its ducts empty into the superior conjunctival fornix.
Lacrimal artery from the ophthalmic artery; superior ophthalmic vein to the cavernous sinus; superficial parotid nodes.
Sensory: lacrimal nerve (V1). Parasympathetic: greater petrosal to pterygopalatine ganglion, stimulating secretion. Sympathetic: superior cervical ganglion via deep petrosal, inhibiting it.
Tears drain: puncta, lacrimal sac, nasolacrimal duct, inferior nasal meatus.
Ciliary ganglion: parasympathetic from CN III; branches are the short ciliary nerves.

high_yield.html: Eyelid layers (5) from outside in: skin and cilia → loose connective/adipose tissue → muscle (orbicularis oculi, levator) → tarsal plate → palpebral conjunctiva.
Levator palpebrae superioris = CN III; its smooth deep part, the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle = sympathetic. Closing the eye = orbicularis oculi = CN VII.
Tear film, 3 layers: oil (meibomian glands) → water (lacrimal gland) → mucin (conjunctival goblet cells).
Tear drainage: lacrimal gland → superior conjunctival fornix → across the cornea → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus.

Lacrimal gland nerves: secretomotor parasympathetic = CN VII → greater petrosal → nerve of pterygoid canal → pterygopalatine ganglion → V2 → zygomatic → lacrimal nerve. Sympathetic (deep petrosal) inhibits. Sensory = lacrimal nerve (V1).
The lacrimal nerve (V1) is sensory; it only hitchhikes the parasympathetic fibres at the end. The parasympathetics come from CN VII, not V.
Glands of Zeis = sebaceous; glands of Moll = modified apocrine sweat glands; meibomian (tarsal) glands make the oil layer. Don't swap them.
The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion for CN III (pupil and ciliary muscle), not for the lacrimal gland. Lacrimal secretion relays in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

Ptosis: complete ptosis → CN III palsy (levator); mild ptosis with a small pupil → Horner syndrome (loss of sympathetic tarsal muscle). The orbital septum separates preseptal (lid) from orbital cellulitis.
A lesion of CN VII before the greater petrosal branch (at or above the geniculate ganglion) gives a dry eye as well as facial palsy; a lesion at the stylomastoid foramen does not.

deeper.title: Why Horner's syndrome gives a drooping eyelid
deeper.html:
Two muscles lift the upper lid. The levator palpebrae superioris is skeletal muscle on CN III and does most of the work. Behind it sits the superior tarsal muscle (Muller's muscle), smooth muscle running from the underside of the levator to the upper border of the tarsus, supplied by sympathetic fibres and worth about 1 to 3 mm of lift. Lose the sympathetic supply, as in Horner's syndrome, and you get a mild ptosis, while a CN III palsy gives a far more dramatic one.

Sources: Brainscape, Orbit and ocular adnexae, eyelids; Brainscape, Boards prep ocular anatomy.

deeper.title: Which gland is blocked: a stye or a chalazion
deeper.html:
The eyelid glands have names because they get blocked. The meibomian glands sit inside the tarsal plate and make the oil layer, so a blocked one gives a firm lump in the lid. The glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands at the base of each lash, and the glands of Moll are apocrine sweat glands next to them, so a blocked one gives a tender swelling right at the lid margin.

Sources: Duke histology, Histology of the eye and eyelid; Brainscape, Eye and eyelid.

deeper.title: Basal versus reflex tears
deeper.html:
The main lacrimal gland in the superotemporal orbit makes the reflex tears, the ones that come with onions or grief. The steady, background wetting of the eye comes largely from accessory lacrimal glands, the glands of Krause in the conjunctival fornix and the glands of Wolfring at the border of the tarsal plate. It explains why an eye can still feel dry even with a healthy main gland.

Source: Brainscape, Physiology of the eyelids.

deeper.title: Why the tear film has to be three layers
deeper.html:
Water alone would neither stick to the cornea nor stay there. The mucin layer from the goblet cells makes the corneal surface wettable so the water spreads instead of beading, and the oil layer from the meibomian glands caps it so it does not evaporate between blinks. Lose either outer layer and the eye is dry even if tear production is normal.

Sources: Duke histology, Histology of the eye and eyelid; lecture slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Pr Hajjij Amal's lecture: the configuration and boundaries of the pharynx, the structure of its wall, the constrictor and longitudinal muscles with their nerves, the three subdivisions, the blood supply, lymphatics and innervation, and the physiology of deglutition. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Funnel-shaped fibromuscular tube, 12 to 14 cm, from the skull base to the oesophagus at C6.
Three subdivisions: nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx.
Buccopharyngeal fascia outside the constrictors; pharyngobasilar fascia on their deep surface.
Three constrictors insert on the median fibrous raphe; the superior also on the pharyngeal tubercle.
Inferior constrictor = thyropharyngeus (pharyngeal plexus and external laryngeal nerve) + cricopharyngeus (recurrent laryngeal nerve).
Three elevators: stylopharyngeus (CN IX), palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus (pharyngeal plexus), all inserting on the thyroid lamina.
All pharyngeal and palatal muscles are vagal except tensor veli palatini (V3) and stylopharyngeus (IX).
Nasopharynx: pharyngeal tonsil, auditory tube, torus tubarius.
Oropharynx: superior constrictor behind, palatine and lingual tonsils.
Laryngopharynx: laryngeal inlet, piriform fossa where foreign bodies lodge.
Ascending pharyngeal artery is the main supply; pharyngeal venous plexus drains to the internal jugular; lymph to the jugulodigastric node.
Sensory: upper pharynx V2 and IX; lower pharynx X.
Deglutition: stage 1 voluntary in the mouth, stages 2 and 3 involuntary.
Stage 2: soft palate and Passavant's ridge close the nasopharyngeal isthmus; aryepiglottic folds close the laryngeal inlet.
Stage 3: thyropharyngeus propels, cricopharyngeus relaxes.

high_yield.html: Pharynx runs from the skull base to C6 (lower border of cricoid), 12-14 cm, and continues as the oesophagus. Three parts: naso-, oro-, laryngopharynx.
Motor rule: every pharyngeal and palatal muscle is on the vagus (pharyngeal plexus) except stylopharyngeus (IX) and tensor veli palatini (V3).
Constrictors (superior, middle, inferior) overlap like stacked flowerpots and insert on the median raphe. Inferior constrictor = thyropharyngeus + cricopharyngeus (upper oesophageal sphincter).
Killian's dehiscence, the weak spot between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus, is where a Zenker's (pharyngeal pouch) diverticulum forms: regurgitation of old food, halitosis.

Nasopharynx: pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), opening of the auditory tube, torus tubarius. Oropharynx: palatine tonsils between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. Laryngopharynx: laryngeal inlet and piriform fossae.
Fish bones lodge in the piriform fossa; the internal laryngeal nerve runs under its mucosa and can be injured. Enlarged adenoids block the auditory tube → otitis media with effusion, mouth breathing.
Sensation: nasopharynx = V2; oropharynx = IX (afferent limb of the gag reflex, efferent = X); laryngopharynx = X.

Swallowing: oral phase voluntary; pharyngeal and oesophageal phases involuntary. The soft palate and Passavant's ridge seal the nasopharynx; the aryepiglottic folds close the laryngeal inlet; cricopharyngeus relaxes to let the bolus into the oesophagus.
The three longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus) all insert on the posterior border of the thyroid lamina and elevate the pharynx and larynx.

deeper.title: Why glue ear is a childhood problem
deeper.html:
The auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx right beside the adenoids. In children the tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal, and the adenoids are large, so infection and obstruction at that opening block ventilation of the middle ear. Fluid collects behind the drum and hearing drops. That is why adenoidectomy and grommets are common childhood operations, and why the lecture puts the tube opening and the pharyngeal tonsil on the same slide.

Source: the lecture's nasopharynx features, read with the auditory tube's role as the middle ear connection.

deeper.title: Why the gap between the constrictors matters
deeper.html:
The constrictors overlap like stacked flowerpots, but the overlap is not complete: a weak area, Killian's dehiscence, lies between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor. If cricopharyngeus fails to relax properly in the third stage of swallowing, pressure pushes the mucosa through that gap and forms a pharyngeal pouch. The anatomy of the inferior constrictor's two parts is exactly what explains it.

Source: the lecture's inferior constrictor table and its third stage of deglutition.

deeper.title: Why a fishbone lodges in the piriform fossa
deeper.html:
The larynx bulges backwards into the laryngopharynx, leaving a gutter on each side. Food is meant to slide down these gutters around the closed laryngeal inlet, which is why they exist. A sharp fragment, though, can catch in the mucosa there instead of passing on. The lecture's clinical note is the reason the piriform fossa is the first place looked at when someone swallows a bone.

Source: the lecture's piriform fossa slide and clinical note.

deeper.title: Why the gag reflex tests two nerves
deeper.html:
Touching the back of the pharynx tests sensation carried by CN IX and the motor response of the constrictors through CN X. That is why the gag reflex is used to assess the two nerves together, and why loss of it, along with a drooping palate, points to a lesion of the vagus or the pharyngeal plexus rather than to a local throat problem.

Source: the lecture's innervation slides.

title: Anatomy of the peripheral nervous system
subject: subj:anat3

provenance.note: The peripheral nervous system.pdf (Anatomy 3, Neuroanatomy lecture 12, Prof. F. Fliyou, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Fliyou's lecture: the organisation of the PNS, the twelve cranial nerves with the olfactory, visual, oculomotor, trigeminal and facial pathways, the spinal nerves and plexuses, the sciatic nerve, the somatic system and reflexes, and the autonomic system with its two divisions and clinical correlations. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: PNS: everything outside brain and cord; 12 cranial and 31 spinal nerve pairs.
Sensory cranial nerves I, II, VIII; motor III, IV, VI, XI, XII; mixed V, VII, IX, X.
Parasympathetic cranial nerves: III, VII, IX, X.
Olfactory axons cross the cribriform plate.
Optic nerve lesion: ipsilateral blindness. Chiasm: bitemporal. Tract or cortex: contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
Trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave; V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale.
Upper face bilateral input, lower face contralateral only.
Facial canal: labyrinthine (narrowest), tympanic, mastoid; exits the stylomastoid foramen; five branches in the parotid.
Plexuses: cervical C1 to C5 (phrenic), brachial C4 to T1, lumbar (femoral), sacral L4 to S4 (sciatic).
Sciatic nerve: L4 to S3, below piriformis, divides near the popliteal fossa.
Somatic motor: one neuron, acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors. Patellar reflex is monosynaptic.
Sympathetic: T1 to L2, noradrenaline post. Parasympathetic: craniosacral, acetylcholine throughout.
Horner's syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis.

high_yield.html: Nerve types: sensory I, II, VIII; motor III, IV, VI, XI, XII; mixed V, VII, IX, X; parasympathetic III, VII, IX, X.
'Standing Room Only': V1 → Superior orbital fissure, V2 → foramen Rotundum, V3 → foramen Ovale. Trigeminal ganglion sits in Meckel's cave.

Visual field lesions: optic nerve = ipsilateral blindness; chiasm = bitemporal hemianopia; optic tract or occipital cortex = contralateral homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing after a posterior cerebral artery stroke).

Facial nerve: UMN lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to the upper face); LMN lesion (Bell's palsy) paralyses the whole half-face. The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest part of the canal.

Plexuses: cervical (phrenic nerve, C3-C5 keeps the diaphragm alive), brachial (radial, axillary, ulnar, median), lumbar (femoral), sacral (sciatic L4-S3, below piriformis, splits into tibial and common fibular).
The lecture lists cervical C1-C5 and brachial C4-T1. Most textbooks give cervical C1-C4 and brachial C5-T1 (C4 joins only in a 'prefixed' plexus). Know your professor's version and the textbook one.

Somatic motor = 1 neuron (ACh on nicotinic receptors). Autonomic = 2 neurons: sympathetic thoracolumbar T1-L2 (short pre, long post, noradrenaline); parasympathetic craniosacral (long pre, short post, ACh).
Sweat glands are sympathetic but use acetylcholine postganglionically; the adrenal medulla receives preganglionic fibres directly.
Horner syndrome (sympathetic chain lesion): ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis on the same side (e.g. apical lung tumour).
Patellar reflex is monosynaptic (L3-L4): it tests one segment's sensory and motor integrity.

deeper.title: Why Bell's palsy closes nothing but a stroke closes the eye
deeper.html:
The facial nucleus part for the upper face receives fibres from both hemispheres, while the lower face part receives only the opposite side. A stroke cuts only one side's input, so the forehead is still driven by the other hemisphere and the patient can wrinkle it and close the eye. A lesion of the facial nerve itself cuts everything below it, so the whole half of the face falls. That one difference tells a stroke apart from Bell's palsy.

Source: the lecture's facial nerve slides on bilateral and contralateral input.

deeper.title: Why sympathetic fibres reach the head from the chest
deeper.html:
Sympathetic outflow only leaves the cord between T1 and L2, yet the eye, face and sweat glands of the head are supplied too. The fibres climb up the sympathetic chain to the superior cervical ganglion, then ride on the carotid arteries into the head. A lesion anywhere along that long route, including a lung apex tumour, can cause Horner's syndrome.

Source: the lecture's sympathetic anatomy and Horner's syndrome slides.

deeper.title: Why diabetic autonomic neuropathy makes you dizzy on standing
deeper.html:
Standing pools blood in the legs, and normally the sympathetic system constricts vessels at once to hold blood pressure. When diabetes damages those autonomic fibres, the reflex fails, pressure drops on standing and the patient feels faint. The same damage explains the bladder and sexual symptoms the lecture lists.

Source: the lecture's clinical correlations slide.

deeper.title: Why a herniated disc causes pain down the leg
deeper.html:
The sciatic nerve is built from the L4 to S3 roots. A disc bulging at the lower lumbar levels presses on one of those roots before it even joins the nerve, and the brain reads the pain as coming from wherever that root supplies, down the back of the thigh and into the leg. That is why the pain of sciatica follows a dermatome rather than staying in the back.

Source: the lecture's sciatic nerve and sciatica slides.

provenance.note: 4. Paranasal sinuses.pdf (Facio-Maxillary Module, Zehra Jamil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows the lecture: the nasal cavity and its lateral wall, then each of the four paranasal sinuses with its relations, nerve and blood supply, and finally the full table of where each one opens. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Nares open onto the face; choanae open into the nasopharynx.
Four air channels: inferior, middle and superior meatuses plus the spheno-ethmoidal recess.
Four sinuses: ethmoidal, sphenoidal, maxillary, frontal. Functions: lighten the skull, add resonance.
Sinuses are rudimentary at birth, enlarge at 6 to 7 years, then after puberty; lined by respiratory epithelium.
Frontal sinus: average 2.5 cm, triangular, drains to the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct, supplied by V1.
Ethmoidal: three sets of cells, 3 to 18 per side; ethmoid bulla from the middle cells; V1 and V2 supply.
Maxillary: the largest, 3.5 x 2.5 x 3.5 cm; roof the inferior orbital margin, floor the alveolus, base the lateral nasal wall, apex the zygomatic process; V2 supply.
Sphenoidal: pituitary and optic chiasma above, cavernous sinus and CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI laterally.
Openings: maxillary, frontal and anterior/middle ethmoidal to the middle meatus; posterior ethmoidal to the superior meatus; sphenoidal to the spheno-ethmoidal recess.
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.

high_yield.html: Where each sinus opens: maxillary, frontal, anterior and middle ethmoidal → middle meatus; posterior ethmoidal → superior meatus; sphenoid → sphenoethmoidal recess. Nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus.
The middle meatus is the busy one: everything except the posterior ethmoid cells and the sphenoid drains there (hiatus semilunaris, ethmoidal infundibulum, bulla).
Maxillary sinus = largest; roof = orbital floor, floor = alveolar process (molar roots), base = lateral nasal wall. Nerve = V2. Frontal sinus = V1.
Sphenoid sinus relations: above = pituitary (sella) and optic chiasm; laterally = cavernous sinus with the ICA and CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI. Basis of trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery.

Sinuses are rudimentary or absent at birth (maxillary and ethmoid are present early; frontal develops by ~7-8 years), enlarging at 6-7 years and after puberty. A frontal sinusitis in a toddler is unlikely.

Sphenoid opening: this lecture says sphenoethmoidal recess; the nasal cavity lecture lists it with the superior meatus region. The recess lies above the superior concha; give 'sphenoethmoidal recess' unless your professor says otherwise.
Maxillary sinusitis drains badly (ostium high on the medial wall) and can mimic upper toothache (shared V2 supply). Ethmoid infection can spread to the orbit through the lamina papyracea.

deeper.title: Why the maxillary sinus drains badly
deeper.html:
Its opening is not at the bottom of the sinus but high up on its base, near the roof. Drainage therefore works against gravity and depends on the cilia of the respiratory epithelium sweeping mucus upward to the ostium. Let that lining swell in a cold and the narrow opening closes, mucus pools, and bacteria follow. It is why the maxillary sinus is the one most often infected.

Source: the lecture's opening table and the pyramidal shape it describes.

deeper.title: Toothache that is really sinusitis
deeper.html:
The floor of the maxillary sinus is the alveolus of the maxilla, so the roots of the upper premolars and molars sit just beneath the sinus, sometimes projecting into it. The same maxillary nerve (V2) supplies both, through its alveolar branches. Inflammation in the sinus can therefore feel exactly like toothache in several upper teeth at once, and a dental infection can break into the sinus.

Source: the lecture's maxillary sinus boundaries and its V2 innervation.

deeper.title: Why the sphenoid sinus is a surgical corridor
deeper.html:
The lecture's list of relations is not idle detail. Because the pituitary sits directly above the sphenoidal sinus, surgeons reach pituitary tumours by going through the nose and the sinus rather than opening the skull: the trans-sphenoidal approach. The same list explains the risk: the internal carotid artery and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI lie in the lateral wall, millimetres away.

Source: the lecture's sphenoidal sinus relations slide.

deeper.title: Why ethmoid infection threatens the eye
deeper.html:
The ethmoidal labyrinth lies between the orbits and the nasal fossae, separated from the orbit only by the lamina papyracea, the paper-thin orbital plate of the ethmoid. Infection in the ethmoidal cells can cross that sheet into the orbit, which is why orbital cellulitis in children most often begins as ethmoid sinusitis.

Source: the lecture's ethmoidal labyrinth description, read with the orbital wall anatomy.

provenance.note: ANATOMY OF SPINAL CORD.pdf (Anatomy 3, Neuroanatomy lecture 7, Prof. F. Fliyou, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Fliyou's lecture: embryology, the external and internal configuration of the cord, the spinal nerves, the canal and meninges, the blood supply, functional anatomy and clinical aspects. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: The spinal cord develops from the caudal neural tube: mantle zone to grey matter, marginal zone to white matter.
Alar plate sensory, basal plate motor, divided by the sulcus limitans; dorsal roots come from the neural crest.
Cord ends at S1 (6 fetal months), L3 (birth), L1/L2 disc (adult).
Length 40 to 45 cm; foramen magnum to L1; conus medullaris, filum terminale to Co1.
31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8, 12, 5, 5, 1.
Enlargements: cervical C4 to T1, lumbar L1 to S3.
Deep anterior median fissure, shallow posterior median sulcus.
Grey matter butterfly: dorsal horn sensory, ventral horn motor, lateral horn autonomic (T1 to L2, S2 to S4).
Dorsal columns carry fine touch and proprioception; spinothalamic carries pain and temperature.
Meninges: dura, arachnoid, pia; CSF in the subarachnoid space; fat and veins in the epidural space.
Denticulate ligament: pial septa anchoring the cord to the dura.
Vertebral artery gives anterior and posterior spinal arteries; 31 pairs of radicular branches.
Lumbar puncture below L3 is safe because only the cauda equina lies there.

high_yield.html: Cord ends at L1/L2 in adults (conus medullaris); at L3 at birth. Below it: the cauda equina in the lumbar cistern. Filum terminale anchors it to the coccyx.
Lumbar puncture below L3 (usually L3/L4 or L4/L5, at the level of the iliac crests = L4): the needle meets floating roots, not cord. In infants go lower still.
31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 C, 12 T, 5 L, 5 S, 1 Co. Enlargements: cervical C4-T1 (upper limbs) and lumbar L1-S3 (lower limbs).
Grey matter butterfly: dorsal horn = sensory; ventral horn = motor; lateral horn = autonomic (sympathetic T1-L2, parasympathetic S2-S4).
Embryology: alar plate → sensory (dorsal); basal plate → motor (ventral), divided by the sulcus limitans. Mantle layer → grey; marginal layer → white. Dorsal root ganglia come from neural crest.
Tracts: dorsal columns = fine touch, vibration, proprioception (ipsilateral in the cord); spinothalamic = pain and temperature (crosses within 1-2 segments); corticospinal = voluntary movement.

Anterior median fissure is deep; the posterior median sulcus is shallow. The epidural space (fat, venous plexus) lies outside the dura; CSF is in the subarachnoid space. Denticulate ligaments = pia to dura.

Cord compression is a neurosurgical emergency: segmental signs at the level, upper motor neuron signs below. Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, lower motor neuron leg weakness.
Anterior spinal artery supplies the front two thirds: its occlusion spares the dorsal columns (touch and position sense preserved) but causes paralysis and loss of pain/temperature below the lesion.

deeper.title: Why spinal level and vertebral level do not match
deeper.html:
Because the cord stopped growing while the spine kept going, cord segments sit higher than the vertebrae of the same name, and the gap widens further down. A spinal segment is not at the vertebra with the same number. This matters for reading MRI and for predicting which segment a fracture at a given vertebra has damaged.

Source: the lecture's embryology slides on the ascent of the cord.

deeper.title: Why the lateral horn stops at L2
deeper.html:
The lateral horn in T1 to L2 holds the whole sympathetic outflow of the body, and S2 to S4 holds the sacral parasympathetic outflow. A lesion between these levels can spare one system and hit the other, and a sacral lesion affects bladder, bowel and sexual function, which is why those are checked in any lower cord injury.

Source: the lecture's internal configuration slide.

deeper.title: Why the anterior spinal artery matters most
deeper.html:
The anterior spinal artery supplies about the front two thirds of the cord, including the motor horns and the spinothalamic tracts, while the paired posterior arteries supply the dorsal columns. Blocking the anterior artery causes paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below the level, with touch and proprioception preserved.

Source: the lecture's blood supply and white matter slides, read together.

deeper.title: Why a cord compression is an emergency
deeper.html:
The lecture calls compression a neurosurgical emergency for a reason: the cord has little room in the canal and a fragile blood supply, so pressure quickly causes ischaemia. Function lost for more than a short time may not come back. That is why new weakness with a sensory level is imaged urgently.

Source: the lecture's practical aspects slides.

provenance.note: Anatomy of the Thyroid Gland EFM2.pdf (Anatomy 4, ENT Anatomy, Pr Hajjij Amal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Pr Hajjij Amal's lecture: the situation and morphology of the gland, the thyroid region and its two capsules, the relations with the laryngo-tracheal axis, the recurrent nerves and the parathyroids, the blood supply and lymphatics, and the physiology of the thyroid and parathyroid glands. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Thyroid: median endocrine gland, infrahyoid region, opposite C5 to T1, behind the strap muscles.
Two lateral lobes plus an isthmus, H or butterfly shaped; lobes 6 cm, isthmus 1 by 1.5 cm, weight about 30 g.
Pyramidal lobe: inconstant, from the upper edge of the isthmus, left of the midline.
True capsule from the gland's own stroma; false capsule from the pretracheal fascia, thickening as the suspensory ligament of Berry to the cricoid.
The venous plexus lies deep to the true capsule, so the capsule is removed with the gland.
Isthmus covers tracheal rings 2, 3 and 4; the lobes cover rings 1 to 5 or 6.
The gland moves with swallowing because the ligaments of Berry tie it to the larynx and trachea.
Right recurrent nerve hooks at the right subclavian artery; the left below the aortic arch.
The right nerve passes in front of the inferior thyroid artery branches; the left behind them.
Both parathyroids lie on the posteromedial border of the lateral lobe, in the fat of the thyroid space.
Superior thyroid artery: first branch of the external carotid. Inferior thyroid artery: from the thyrocervical trunk.
Superior and middle thyroid veins to the internal jugular; inferior thyroid veins to the left brachiocephalic vein.
Lymph: median collectors to prelaryngeal or pretracheal nodes; lateral collectors to the jugular nodes.
Thyroid hormones from follicular cells; calcitonin from C cells, hypocalcemic.
Parathyroid hormone: hypercalcemic and hypophosphoremic.

high_yield.html: Two lobes + isthmus. Isthmus over tracheal rings 2-4. Level C5-T1. Pyramidal lobe (inconstant) = remnant of the thyroglossal duct.
Two capsules: true capsule (gland's own stroma) and false capsule (pretracheal fascia), which thickens as the ligament of Berry to the cricoid. That is why a thyroid lump moves up on swallowing.
The venous plexus lies deep to the true capsule, so the true capsule is removed with the gland (the opposite of the prostate).
Arteries: superior thyroid = first branch of the external carotid; inferior thyroid = thyrocervical trunk (subclavian). Veins: superior and middle → internal jugular; inferior → left brachiocephalic.

Surgical pairs: the external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery (ligate close to the gland); the recurrent laryngeal nerve is related to the inferior thyroid artery (ligate away from the gland).

Right recurrent nerve passes in front of the inferior thyroid artery branches; left passes behind them (this lecture's description). Anatomy here is variable, which is exactly why the nerve is at risk.
Parathyroids sit on the posteromedial border of each lobe. Removing them in thyroidectomy → hypocalcaemia (tingling, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs).
Hormones: follicular cells → T3/T4; C cells → calcitonin (lowers Ca²⁺); parathyroid → PTH (raises Ca²⁺, lowers phosphate).

Strap (infrahyoid) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid (deep to sternohyoid), thyrohyoid, omohyoid; supplied by C1-C3 (ansa cervicalis). They lie in front of the gland; tracheostomy goes through the midline between them.

deeper.title: Why a thyroid lump moves when you swallow
deeper.html:
The ligaments of Berry tie the gland to the cricoid cartilage and the first tracheal rings, and the whole larynx rides upward during swallowing. Any swelling of the thyroid therefore moves up with it. That single sign separates a thyroid mass from most other neck lumps at the bedside, and it follows directly from the lecture's relations slides.

Source: the lecture's relation with the laryngo-tracheal axis and the ligaments of Berry.

deeper.title: Why the two recurrent nerves behave differently in surgery
deeper.html:
The lecture separates the right and left nerves for a reason. The right hooks around the subclavian artery high in the neck and runs a more oblique course, often in front of the inferior thyroid artery branches. The left loops under the aortic arch in the chest and ascends almost vertically in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, usually behind those branches. A surgeon looking for the nerve therefore looks in a different place on each side.

Source: the lecture's two slides on the right and left inferior laryngeal nerves.

deeper.title: Why hoarseness after thyroid surgery is investigated urgently
deeper.html:
The recurrent nerve supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid. Injure one and the cord on that side sits paramedian and does not vibrate, giving a hoarse voice. Injure both and the cords sit paramedian together, which threatens the airway rather than just the voice. That risk is why the lecture calls the relation with the recurrent nerves a major hazard of thyroidectomy.

Source: the lecture's emphasis on recurrent nerve risk, read with the larynx lecture's account of nerve palsies.

deeper.title: Why the parathyroids are the other surgical worry
deeper.html:
The parathyroids are small, orange-yellow and sit in the fat right on the posteromedial border of the lobe, sometimes within the tissue the surgeon is removing. Take them all and the patient loses parathyroid hormone, calcium falls and tetany follows. The lecture pairs them with the recurrent nerves for exactly this reason: both are small, both are close, and both change the patient's life if lost.

Source: the lecture's parathyroid gland slides and its introduction.

title: Anatomy of the ventricles and CSF
subject: subj:anat3

provenance.note: 7. anatomy of ventricules and cerebrospinal fluid.pdf (Anatomy 3, Neuroanatomy lecture 8, Prof. F. Fliyou, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Ventricles: 2 lateral, third, cerebral aqueduct, fourth.
Lateral ↔ third: foramina of Monro. Third ↔ fourth: aqueduct of Sylvius (midbrain).
Fourth → subarachnoid space: Magendie (median, to cisterna magna) and Luschka (2 lateral, to cerebellopontine cisterns).
Lateral ventricle: frontal, temporal, occipital horns, body, atrium; C-shaped.
Frontal horn: septum pellucidum medially, head of caudate laterally, genu of corpus callosum in front.
Temporal horn: longest and largest, ends at the amygdala, hippocampus in the floor.
Third ventricle: between the thalami; floor = optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies.
Fourth ventricle: behind the brainstem, in front of the cerebellum; floor = rhomboid fossa.
Sulcus limitans: motor nuclei medial, sensory lateral.
No choroid plexus in the frontal and occipital horns or the aqueduct.
CSF: about 150 mL in total (125 subarachnoid, 25 ventricles); about 500 mL made a day.
Absorption: arachnoid granulations (Pacchioni) into the superior sagittal sinus.
Pia is the only meningeal layer that follows the gyri.
Hydrocephalus: communicating (absorption or production) versus non-communicating (obstruction, often the aqueduct).
ETV opens the floor of the third ventricle into the interpeduncular cistern.
Lumbar puncture at L3-L4 or L4-L5; the cord ends at L1-L2.

high_yield.html: The pipe: choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → Monro → third → aqueduct (Sylvius) → fourth → Magendie (cisterna magna) and Luschka (cerebellopontine cisterns) → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → superior sagittal sinus.
Magendie = Median, Luschka = Lateral (two of them).

Third ventricle floor, front to back: optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies. Anterior wall: fornix columns, anterior commissure, lamina terminalis. Posterior wall: habenular commissure, pineal, posterior commissure.

Lateral ventricle: frontal horn has the septum pellucidum medially and head of caudate laterally; the temporal horn is the longest and largest, ends at the amygdala, with the hippocampus in its floor; the tapetum separates the temporal and occipital horns from the optic radiations.
Fourth ventricle: behind the brainstem, in front of the cerebellum; floor = rhomboid fossa; sulcus limitans: motor medial, sensory lateral; caudal tip = obex.
No choroid plexus in the frontal and occipital horns or the aqueduct. CSF: about 150 mL present (125 subarachnoid, 25 ventricular), about 500 mL made a day.

Hydrocephalus: everything upstream of a block dilates. Aqueduct block = lateral and third ventricles large, fourth normal (non-communicating). All four large with no block = absorption problem (communicating). Rare overproduction: choroid plexus papilloma.
Treatment: ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or ETV (floor of the third ventricle → interpeduncular cistern; only bypasses blocks below the third ventricle).
Lumbar puncture at L3-L4 or L4-L5: the adult cord ends at about L1-L2, but the subarachnoid space continues below.

deeper.title: Work out hydrocephalus from the block
deeper.html:
Every hydrocephalus question becomes easy if you draw the pipe. Everything upstream of a block swells; everything downstream stays normal. A block at one foramen of Monro dilates one lateral ventricle. A block at the aqueduct dilates both lateral ventricles and the third, with a normal fourth ventricle. A block at the fourth ventricle outlets dilates all four. If all four are large and nothing is blocked, the problem is absorption (or production): communicating hydrocephalus.

This also explains ETV: a hole in the floor of the third ventricle lets CSF skip an aqueduct block, so it only works when the obstruction is below the third ventricle.

Source: the lecture's hydrocephalus and ETV slides; Kenhub, Ventricles of the brain.

deeper.title: Why CSF is renewed several times a day
deeper.html:
About 500 mL is made each day but only about 150 mL is present at any moment, so the whole volume turns over several times a day. That steady flow is what washes waste out of the brain, and it is also why any obstruction quickly raises pressure: production does not stop when drainage does.

Source: the lecture's CSF physiology slides; Radiopaedia, Cerebrospinal fluid.

figure.alt: The pathway of cerebrospinal fluid
figure.caption: CSF is made by the choroid plexus and flows one way, from the lateral ventricles to the venous sinuses. Schematic drawn for this site.
